The title marks a staff study on a new stage in the split between Moscow and Beijing. Its trailing month breaks off at Octob in the heading. The brief record is a staff study item from 1962.
cia-0000112344: Ufo Research Organization to Hold Conference in Beijing is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112344, dated March 4, 1992. The title reports a planned conference in Beijing by a UFO research organization. The organization is not named in the heading itself. The brief record is a conference item, filed in the spring of 1992 as released in the files.
cia-0000119744: A CIA report gives the Hungarian situation as of 1 a.m. Eastern time during the 1956 crisis. Overnight editions like this one kept Washington posted while Budapest slept, and the paper preserves that early morning picture of the revolt. Hour-stamped reports from that autumn survive as a minute-by-minute layer in the record of the uprising, each one fixing what was known when.
cia-0000132144: An August 1988 CIA Middle East Brief for August 18 carries a Pakistan situation report: a crash has killed the Pakistani president and the American ambassador. President Zia-ul-Haq died in that crash the day before. The brief covers the crisis as it broke. Zia's death left Pakistan's course suddenly open, and a same-week brief on the crash belongs to the first hours of a succession no one had scripted.
cia-0000132444:
A proposed Cuban conference of underdeveloped nations fills a CIA document dated January 4, 1960. Havana wanted to gather poor countries together and speak as their leader. The idea of a third world standing apart from both Cold War camps was still new at the time.

The document covers the proposal and the planning behind it. Cuba hoped the meeting would raise its standing far beyond the Caribbean. For readers, the entry shows the young revolution thinking globally from its first year. It also shows Washington watching that ambition closely and counting which governments might answer Havana's call.
cia-0000132644: Central American republics possibly acting together to break relations fill a CIA item dated May 1, 1960. The headline breaks off at the word relati, plainly meaning relations with Cuba. Joint action was the playbook regional bodies used on the Cuba problem. A shared break would isolate Havana across the isthmus at once. The short item reports the possible move and its backers.
cia-0000132744:
The running series Cuban Developments continued on November 4, 1960, four days before the American presidential election. By late 1960 the break between Washington and Castro was effectively complete. The United States was backing Cuban exiles against his government.

Against that backdrop, the series kept its steady watch: regular entries recording the revolution's course while policy hardened around it. The November paper stands between the summer's collapsing relations and the new year, when planning turned to invasion. Now open to the public, the declassified briefing preserves one entry in that unbroken watch. The watch itself continued without pause.
cia-0000134244: Dated 1961, this declassified CIA item is a letter addressed to the Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs, the president's top national security aide. The catalog title is cut off mid-word, and it gives neither a sender nor a subject. The record does not say what the letter concerns, so no subject is claimed. It is preserved as released through the CIA Reading Room, a piece of correspondence to the White House whose text must speak for itself.
cia-0000135744: Dated 4 March 1961, a Spanish text from the papers of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was nearing the end of its training for the invasion of Cuba, which the CIA had organized in secret over the previous year. The catalog record names no subject for this document. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of a close run of brigade items from the first days of March 1961.
cia-0000136144: A declassified CIA cable dated 2 April 1954 turns to sending a Spanish text cable directed toward a reader the heading leaves cut off. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136344: Castillo needed twenty thousand quetzales urgently, according to the radio material from the night of 28 June 1954 summarized in this cable. Weather had improved, he had a patrol southwest of Zacapa, and another force was told to aid a maneuver by attacking Zacapa from the west. Other messages report railway bridges over the Tamaras and Uluazapa rivers that must be blown to stop night supply shipments. The war was ending, but the orders kept flowing.
cia-0000136744: Dated 4 February 1961, a Spanish text from the papers of Brigade 2506. The exile force was drilling through its final winter, weeks from embarkation. The catalog record gives this document no individual subject. It survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, a dated unit in the brigade's February archive, and it is described here on the strength of the record alone.
cia-0000139044: Hans Berger reviews Walter Lippmann in this September 1944 OSS note. The heading calls it a German communist view of Germany. Berger held an important rank in the international communist movement. He praised Lippmann's earlier book on foreign policy. It stressed ending isolationism once and for all. The new book draws his fire. Lippmann offers an ersatz system of orbits, Berger argues. Germany would be made dependent on maritime commerce. It would sit inside an Atlantic Community. Berger calls it a Chamberlain thesis in new garb.
cia-03189344: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/06/25, a CIA publication. A further June briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-06232644: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/11/20, a CIA publication. The November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06714444: COLLECTION GAME ROLES, a CIA document. The gaming roles. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
coke-institutes-part4-1644:
The Fourth Part of Coke's Institutes was printed in 1644, in the heat of the English Civil War. Its subject is the jurisdiction of courts: which court may hear which kind of case. Coke, who had presided over the system he describes, maps the whole machinery of English justice.

He surveys courts from Parliament and the great courts at Westminster down to local and special tribunals. For each, he gives its powers, its officers, and its limits. The survey doubles as a defense of the common law courts against rival royal courts of his own day. Read as a whole, the volume is the constitution of England in legal dress, an institutional map drawn by the man who knew the terrain best. It completes Coke's great design for the Institutes.
doe-osti-3010790-final-technical-report-: DE-SC0020144 got its technical finale, and this DOE final covers the award closeout. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their record. The award was DE-SC0020144. The record was researcher. The closeout was award. The report was technical.
doe-osti-3362717-final-report-sc0022244: SC0022244 got finally reported, and this DOE final covers the report. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was researcher. The SC0022244 were final. The researchers were closeout. The report were final.
dumas-corsican-brothers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Corsican Brothers in 1844, here in Henry Frith's English translation. The eerie tale is the definitive literary treatment of the Corsican blood feud in fiction. Dumas had toured Corsica and filled the tale with its wild hills and stern codes.

Twin brothers, joined at birth and split by surgery, still share each other's pains across distance. One lives a Paris dandy, the other a mountain man bound to vendetta and honor in Corsica. A duel over a woman in Paris is felt, wound for wound, by the brother at home. The surviving twin takes up the feud, and the debt of blood is paid in full. Frith's version kept the tale a staple of English Gothic and sensation shelves.
dumas-count-of-monte-cristo-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Count of Monte Cristo in 1844, in serial form in Paris. The vast tale of betrayal and revenge became one of the world's most popular novels ever. Dumas drew its germ from a police file tale of a man falsely jailed for years.

Edmond Dantès, a young sailor, is jailed on his wedding day by rivals' false charges. In the Château d'If, Abbé Faria teaches him and tells of a vast treasure on Monte Cristo. Dantès escapes, finds the gold, and returns as the Count to ruin his three betrayers. Each revenge is patient, rich, and exact, yet mercy checks his hand at the brink. The book's grip on readers, from schoolboys to statesmen, has never loosened since 1844.
dumas-regents-daughter-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Regent's Daughter in 1844, opening his Regency cycle of historical romance. The tale retells the Cellamare conspiracy against the Regent, Philippe d'Orléans, in early 1700s France. It appeared the same year as The Three Musketeers, in Dumas's flood of serial triumphs then.

Gaston de Chanlay, a Breton noble, joins a Spanish-backed plot to kidnap the Regent in Paris. He loves Hélène, a convent girl who proves to be the Regent's own hidden daughter in secret. Duty to the plot and love for Hélène tear the young conspirator in two at Paris. The Regent's mercy and the block await the plotters in a close of mixed grace. Dumas finds pathos in a minor plot that most histories pass in a page.
dumas-three-musketeers-1844:
Alexandre Dumas published The Three Musketeers in 1844, in serial form in a Paris paper. The swashbuckling tale of d'Artagnan and his three friends became a byword for adventure in France. Its motto, all for one and one for all, is known far beyond the book.

Young d'Artagnan rides to Paris with a letter, a horse, and dreams of the King's Musketeers. He falls in with Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, and duels become brotherhood in a single day. Queen Anne's diamond studs, Richelieu's plots, and the spy Milady drive the swift intrigue along. The siege of La Rochelle gives the private vendettas a grand public stage of war. Dumas's pace, humor, and swordplay still set the bar for historical adventure tales.
emerson-essays-second-series-1844:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: Second Series in 1844, with The Poet and Experience inside. The set is the mature statement of transcendentalist aesthetics in Emerson's evolving and deepening public thought. Grief for his dead son darkens Experience, giving the later essays a chastened, autumnal tone throughout them.

The Poet calls for an American bard who will sing the facts of farms, trades, and rivers. Experience asks what life teaches when sorrow shows how little the soul can truly hold fast. Character, Manners, and Gifts weigh how spirit shows in conduct, breeding, and the things we give. Emerson's sentences here are denser, more oracular, and less sure than in the first bright series. Whitman and later poets took The Poet as a personal commission to write America.
europmc-pmc10029244:
Zhang and co-workers review the roles of tumor-linked macrophages in checkpoint immunotherapy for solid cancers, in a 2023 paper. Checkpoint drugs free T cells to attack tumors, yet only a small share of patients gains lasting benefit. The cells around the tumor, including macrophages, help decide who responds.

The review explains how these macrophages can block or aid the drugs' effects. It surveys ways to reprogram them, such as blocking their signals or clearing them out. The authors argue that pairing such steps with checkpoint drugs could widen the circle of patients who benefit.
europmc-pmc10172144:
Gordon and a large team report that a body-and-mind action network alternates with movement zones in the motor cortex, in a 2023 study. The motor cortex is the brain strip that controls movement. Textbooks drew it as a smooth map running from foot to face, yet hints of a more complex layout had built up for years.

Using precise brain imaging, the team found zones for whole-body action planning wedged between zones for single body parts. The finding rewrites a classic brain map. It may also help explain links between movement, thought, and body control.
europmc-pmc10543444:
Panwar and co-authors reviewed the mTOR signal path in 2023, a master switch for cell growth. mTOR is an enzyme that steers fuel use, growth, survival, and cell movement. It works in two teams, called mTORC1 and mTORC2. It also controls autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process.

When the path sticks on, harm can follow across the body. Panwar links such faults to ageing, brain disease, and many cancers. The path also feeds cancer stem cells and drug resistance. Long non-coding RNAs, gene strips that build no protein, tune the path as well. The review weighs drugs that block mTOR for cancer care. It asks how to make them hit harder in clinics.
europmc-pmc10599644:
Wang, Wang, Yang, and Liu reviewed in 2023 how gut microbes may shape brain growth in children. Microbes in the gut talk to the brain through a two-way route, the microbiota-gut-brain axis. That talk steers body processes as the brain forms. Faults in the talk may feed disorders of brain growth.

Three paths carry the signals, Wang reports: immune, nerve, and hormone routes. The paths overlap and cross-talk as they run. Studies now link the axis to autism, ADHD, and Rett syndrome, a rare growth disorder. The review sums up what each link rests on. It also flags where proof is thin and what tests come next.
europmc-pmc11701544:
Paysan-Lafosse and a large team update the Pfam protein families database in this 2025 paper. Pfam groups proteins into families and domains, the reusable parts of proteins, to aid genome annotation and protein study. Since 2020 the old Pfam website was shut and the resource folded into InterPro, a larger hub.

Curation grew for families from metagenomes, meaning DNA read straight from the environment, and for microproteins and repeat-rich families. The scheme was harmonised with the ECOD structural classification. AlphaFold structure predictions now help refine domain boundaries and spot new domains. Large-scale scans of AlphaFold models found new families. A deep learning add-on, Pfam-N, widened coverage, lifting coverage of the UniProtKB protein archive by 8.8 percent. More frequent releases are planned.
europmc-pmc1240944:
Gurgueira and co-authors exposed rats to concentrated city air particles in 2002. Dish studies had hinted that reactive oxygen species drive particle harm. Whether breathing particles raises those species in living tissue was untested. Rats breathed concentrated particles or filtered air for up to five hours.

After five hours, oxidant signals rose sharply in lung and heart tissue. Lung readings hit 41 counts versus 24 in clean-air controls. Heart readings showed the same jump, while liver showed none. Toxic fly ash particles raised lung readings still higher. Inert carbon black caused no such rise.
europmc-pmc1298944:
Wendler and co-authors tested whether minorities refuse health research more often in 2006. The claim is widespread in the United States. Hard data behind it were scarce. A full literature search found every study reporting consent by race or ethnicity.

Twenty studies covered over 70,000 enrollment decisions. Research types ran from interviews to drug and surgical trials. Most studies were American, with two large multi-country exceptions. Consent patterns were compared across groups study by study. Wendler checks a repeated assumption against the actual record. Most of the twenty studies were single-site American studies.
europmc-pmc1343544:
Olssøn, Mykletun, and Dahl tested an anxiety and depression scale in general practice in 2005. Family doctors often miss generalized anxiety and major depression. Short questionnaires could sharpen their detection. The scale tested was the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Rating Scale.

Survey data covered 1,781 patients of 141 doctors across Norway. Patient-rated reference questionnaires defined true cases. For anxiety, the best cutoff was a score of 8 or more. At that cutoff, sensitivity was 0.89 and specificity 0.75. The scale was also compared against doctor severity ratings. Data were gathered over three days in September 2001.
europmc-pmc1397844:
Zwakhalen, Hamers, Abu-Saad, and Berger reviewed pain scales for severe dementia in 2006. Pain affects 40 to 80 percent of elderly nursing home residents. People with severe dementia cannot report pain directly. Behavior-based scales are the main assessment route.

The search covered four databases plus citations from 1988 to 2005. Twenty-nine publications on behavioral tools were selected. Twelve watch-based scales were evaluated for measurement quality and clinical use. Named scales include PAINAD, PACSLAC, and DOLOPLUS2. Quality criteria judged reliability and validity of each scale. Zwakhalen guides tool choice for dementia care. Scales were judged for use in daily care too. Pain checks are step one in good pain care for these old people. Good tools must be quick for staff to use at the bed side.
europmc-pmc1435944:
Linking a gene to a disease takes many kinds of proof. Yue, Melamud, and Moult built a web tool for that task in 2006, called SNPs3D. One part names genes that may drive a chosen disease. A second part shows how those genes relate to each other.

A third part judges how a single letter change, a SNP, may harm a protein. It uses protein shape and clues from how species keep the spot alike. Each gene page links to papers, activity data, and mouse studies. Yue shows the tool at work on swelling responses and high blood pressure, helping users form testable models fast.
europmc-pmc1698944:
A common cold-sore kin rewires a cell's chemistry to feed its own copying. Munger and co-authors measured that rewiring in 2006 during human cytomegalovirus infection of fibroblasts. They tracked 63 metabolites over time with mass spectrometry.

As infection advanced, metabolites in sugar burning, the citric acid cycle, and pyrimidine building climbed markedly. Gene activity for the matching enzymes rose in parallel. Peak levels far exceeded those in growing or resting uninfected cells. Munger concludes the virus imposes its own metabolic program, quite unlike normal cell states, to secure energy and building blocks.
europmc-pmc1866244:
Van Ert, Keim and co-authors charted the world family tree of the anthrax bacterium in 2007. Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax in animals and people, and its global spread was long known only from anecdotes. Typing its strains precisely also matters for tracing outbreaks and attacks.

The team sequenced seven diverse strains end to end to find rare single-letter DNA differences. Those markers, plus 15 repeat-length markers, were used to type 1,033 isolates from 42 countries. The collection split into three known major lineages, then 12 clonal sub-lineages, and finally 221 unique genotypes. Variation proved very rare, as expected for a recently emerged clone. The map documents how the bacterium evolved and diversified as it spread around the world with livestock trade.
europmc-pmc1885944:
Keays, Flint and colleagues traced in 2007 a mouse brain defect to a fault in a skeleton protein, then found the human counterpart. Building the brain requires neurons to migrate into neat layers, and failures cause lissencephaly, a smooth-brain disorder in children. A chemically mutagenized mouse strain showed scrambled layers in cortex and hippocampus.

The fault sat in the energy-binding pocket of alpha-1 tubulin, a building block of the cell's internal rails. It disturbed pairing of tubulin units, which neurons need to move. The match with known lissencephaly models prompted screening of patients with developmental brain anomalies. Two patients carried brand-new mutations in TUBA3, the human version of the mouse gene. The study shows mouse mutagenesis can crack open the basis of human brain disorders.
europmc-pmc1892244:
Schmierer, Miller and co-authors tested in 2007 whether an advanced MRI method truly reflects tissue damage in multiple sclerosis brain after death. Standard MRI predicts patients' disability poorly, likely because it is not specific to the damage that matters. Diffusion tensor imaging, which tracks water movement along nerve fibers, promised better specificity.

They scanned unfixed post mortem MS brain on a standard 1.5-tesla machine, then measured myelin, axon counts, and scarring under the microscope. Both diffusion measures came out lower after death than in living scans. Still, the known contrast held: lesions showed freer water movement and less directionality than normal-looking white matter. Myelin content correlated strongly with both measures, including a correlation of minus 0.79 for the directionality index, and with axon counts as well.
europmc-pmc2064944:
Warady and Chadha reviewed chronic kidney disease in children worldwide in 2007. Knowledge of care has grown through large studies, yet basic counts of how many children are affected remain limited and imprecise. Methods differ between data sources, making comparisons hard. Causes also vary by region, shaped by environment, ancestry, genetics and marriage within families.

Nearly half of childhood cases come from birth defects of the kidney and urinary tract. These include blocked urine flow and underdeveloped kidneys. Kidney transplant is the favoured final treatment for children. But scarce health resources and high death rates in poorer countries limit dialysis and transplant provision. That in turn skews global patient counts. The authors call for better worldwide tracking of the disease in children.
europmc-pmc2065844:
Al-Sakere and co-workers reported in 2007 the first successful use of irreversible electroporation to destroy tumours in mice. The method uses short, strong electric pulses to open permanent holes in cell membranes. Unlike heat or freezing methods, it kills without cooking tissue. Maths models of the electric and heat fields guided a protocol with minimal heating. Aggressive skin tumours were implanted in mice for the test.

Tissue studies confirmed tumours died directly from permanent membrane damage. Success depended on field strength, total pulse length and pulse timing. The best setting used plate electrodes giving 80 pulses of 100 microseconds at 2,500 volts per centimetre. That treatment fully cleared 12 of 13 tumours, a 92 percent success rate, with no tissue heating. The authors present it as a new non-thermal ablation option.
europmc-pmc2100144:
Baral, Sifakis, Cleghorn and Beyrer reviewed HIV risk in 2007 among men who have sex with men living in poorer countries. Reports from the former Soviet Union, Asia, Africa and Latin America showed high infection rates in this group. The team systematically reviewed studies from 2000 to 2006 across low- and middle-income countries. They pooled prevalence data and compared risk with general adult populations.

Risk was far higher for these men in nearly every setting. The pooled odds ratio reached 58.4 in very low-prevalence countries, and 14.4 in low-prevalence ones. It fell to 9.6 where HIV was common. That is still a nine-fold excess, and it remained after pooling across all of the regions studied in this review. By region, the Americas showed the highest ratio at 33.3, and Africa the lowest at 3.8, and the authors call this group understudied and underserved.
europmc-pmc2124944: A medical paper with complete balance studies of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium. The body's elements. This article preserves that metabolism research. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125544: A medical paper on extirpation of the thymus in the guinea pig. The removed gland. This article preserves that immunology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125644: A medical paper with experimental studies upon lymphocytes and immune sera action. The white cells, attacked. This article preserves that immunology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131444: A medical paper on the pathogenesis of early obstructive jaundice. The blocked bile's yellowing. This article preserves that pathology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140444: A biology paper on the relation between the wavelength of light and its effect on photosensors. The light's color. This article preserves that photobiology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140544: A biology paper on the stability of bacterial suspensions, agglutination in the presence of salts. The clumping germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. Later readers can locate it. It retains its place in time. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2265044:
Calafat, Ye, Wong, Reidy and Needham measured the antibacterial chemical triclosan in 2008 in urine from a national United States survey. Triclosan is used widely in soaps, toothpaste, textiles and kitchen plastics. The team analysed 2,517 urine samples from the 2003-2004 survey of people aged six and older, using automated extraction and mass spectrometry. They compared levels across age, income, race and sex groups.

Triclosan was detected in 74.6 percent of samples, spanning concentrations from 2.4 to 3,790 micrograms per litre. The geometric mean was 13.0 micrograms per litre, while the 95th percentile reached 459.0 on the same scale. A minority thus carry far higher body burdens than typical. Levels peaked in the third decade of life. People in high-income households had significantly higher levels than lower-income groups. Race and sex showed no differences.
europmc-pmc2395244:
Haas and colleagues introduced an automated gene-finding tool for complex genomes in 2008. Annotating a genome means marking where each gene starts, ends, and is spliced. For eukaryotes, organisms with a cell nucleus, doing this by hand is far too slow, and single computer programs often disagree.

Their tool, EVidenceModeler, weighs predictions from many sources and merges them into one best gene model for each region. A partner program, the Program to Assemble Spliced Alignments, feeds it evidence from aligned gene transcripts. Together they predict protein-coding regions, alternative splice forms, where one gene yields several message versions, and the untranslated regions at message ends. The authors offered the pair as a standard pipeline for new genome projects.
europmc-pmc2556744:
De Backer and fellow specialists reported in 2007 the consensus of a round table conference on how to judge the microcirculation, the body's smallest blood vessels. Faults there help drive organ failure in critical illness, especially sepsis, and new cameras let doctors watch these vessels directly. But laboratories scored the images in incompatible ways, so the group met in Amsterdam to agree on standards.

They fixed five rules for good imaging. Sample five sites per organ. Avoid pressing on the tissue. Clear away secretions. Keep focus and contrast right. Check recording quality. Scoring should report vessel density and the share of vessels carrying flow. It should also report a flow index and a heterogeneity index for how uneven flow is. Values should be given separately for vessels under 20 micrometres wide, the true capillaries.
europmc-pmc2633044:
Depienne and colleagues identified in 2009 a second gene behind a Dravet-like epileptic encephalopathy of infancy. Dravet syndrome, a severe seizure disorder with developmental regression, is usually caused by mutations in SCN1A, but 27 percent of the team's patients tested negative. Screening 41 such patients with dense gene chips uncovered a deletion removing the PCDH19 gene on the X chromosome in one boy.

Sequencing PCDH19 in 73 more negative patients found nine different mutations in 11 unrelated girls. The boy's skin cells proved mosaic: only some cells carried the deletion. That supports a cellular interference mechanism for this female-predominant disorder. Patients with PCDH19 mutations closely resembled Dravet cases. They had early fever-linked seizures in clusters and language delays. But their myoclonic jerks and atypical absences were rarer.
europmc-pmc2653744:
Wolin and colleagues combined results from 52 studies in 2009 to measure how much physical activity lowers the risk of colon cancer. The link between exercise and lower risk was well known, but no up-to-date pooled number existed. The team searched the literature through June 2008 and kept only studies that reported colon cancer on its own.

Across the studies, the most active people had about a 24 percent lower risk than the least active. The benefit looked much the same for men and for women. Studies that asked patients to recall past activity after diagnosis showed a stronger effect than studies that followed healthy people forward in time. The authors note plausible reasons: less inflammation, faster passage of food through the gut, and lower insulin levels in active people.
europmc-pmc2708144:
Evans reviewed in 2009 neurofibromatosis type 2, a rare inherited disorder that grows tumors on nerves and in the brain and spine. About one person in sixty thousand has it, and most first notice one-sided hearing loss or ringing in the ear. Tumors on both hearing nerves are its hallmark and often lead to deafness.

The review covers other tumors such as meningiomas, growths on the coverings of the brain, plus eye signs like cataracts and skin lumps. Faults in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 cause it, and over half of cases are new faults, not inherited ones. Surgery stays the main treatment, with watchful scans for slow tumors.
europmc-pmc2756044:
Devaraj and co-authors showed in 2007 how the SARS coronavirus blocks the innate interferon defense in infected lung cells. SARS, a severe contagious respiratory disease, induces only a weak interferon response in culture, and its key transcription factor IRF-3 is not activated. Whether the virus hides from sensors or actively counteracts defenses was uncertain.

Searching viral proteins, they found the papain-like protease domain is a potent interferon antagonist, and its protease activity is not even required. The domain binds IRF-3 and blocks its phosphorylation and move into the nucleus, cutting off type I interferon production through two sensing pathways. That sabotage may help SARS-CoV establish infection before adaptive immunity can respond.
europmc-pmc2816644:
Buffa, Harris, West, and Miller built a shared gene signature in 2010 for low oxygen inside tumors, a state called hypoxia that drives growth and resists therapy. Signatures trained on one cancer often fail in others, so the team hunted for one that holds across cancers. They combined known oxygen-sensitive genes with activity patterns from eight cancer datasets, three for head and neck tumors and five for breast tumors.

Genes that rose and fell together with the known oxygen genes across all datasets formed the signature, and it predicted patient outcomes in combined analyses. A trimmed version using only the top few genes, including VEGFA, beat both the full signature and older published ones in fresh head, breast, and lung data.
europmc-pmc2846344:
Fernández-Riejos and colleagues reviewed in 2010 how leptin, the fullness hormone released by fat cells, switches on and shapes the immune system. Fat tissue acts as an active hormone organ, and leptin ties nutritional state to immune strength. Low leptin states come with higher infection risk, while too much leptin accompanies immune attacks on the body's own tissues.

The review gathers lab and clinical evidence that leptin touches nearly every immune branch: it rallies first-response cells, shapes T cell behavior, and fuels inflammation when oversupplied in obesity. The hormone thus sits at the crossing of feeding, energy balance, and defense, helping explain why both starvation and heavy obesity weaken or distort immune responses.
europmc-pmc2860244:
Pardo and co-authors built in 2010 a much larger map of proteins that bind Oct4, the master switch of embryo stem cells. Working in mouse embryo stem cells, they pulled down Oct4 with its attached partners and named them with sensitive protein tools. The study ran in parallel with related work and widened the known Oct4 circle greatly.

Half of the partner proteins are themselves controlled by Oct4 or by fellow stem cell switches, which weaves a tight feedback web. About a third change their levels sharply once cells start to specialize. Most partners tested so far kill early embryos when mutated in mice. Some human versions are already tied to birth defects or to cancer, which gives the map medical reach.
europmc-pmc2901944:
Perencevich and colleagues measured in 2003 what surgical site infections cost when they surface after the patient has gone home, which is when most appear. They followed over forty-five hundred operations and confirmed post-discharge infection in about two percent. Infected patients and matched controls reported their health and care use across the eight weeks after surgery.

Infection brought significantly more outpatient and emergency visits, imaging, readmissions, and home health aide hours. Total costs over the eight weeks averaged about five thousand one hundred dollars per infected patient against roughly one thousand eight hundred for controls, nearly triple. Mental health scores also fell only in the infected group. Hospitals that stop counting at discharge miss most of the true burden of these infections.
europmc-pmc2907344:
Smith and co-authors pooled in 2010 fifty-five randomized trials to pin down how much anthracycline chemotherapy drugs endanger the heart. These drugs are staples against breast and ovarian cancer, lymphoma, myeloma, and sarcoma, but they can damage heart muscle early or years later. Trials of alternative regimens let the team compare clinical heart failure and silent damage rates directly.

Regimens built on anthracyclines carried over five times the odds of clinical heart toxicity of non-anthracycline regimens. europmc-pmc2913244:
Theveneau and colleagues worked out in 2010 how a cluster of embryonic cells migrates toward a chemical beacon without breaking apart. Neural crest cells, among the embryo's most mobile, travel in streams and their movement resembles cancer invasion. A chemokine called Sdf1 attracts the cluster, but single cells alone barely respond, which posed the puzzle.

Filming the cells showed Sdf1 does not create direction from scratch; it stabilizes the polarity that cell contact already sets up. Where two cells touch, the adhesion molecule N-cadherin damps the protrusion machinery, while the free outer edge stays active and extends. The beacon amplifies that front-back difference until the whole group crawls toward it. Contact inhibition of movement, once seen as a brake, turns out to steer collective travel.
europmc-pmc2939644:
Leung, Lam, and Chan checked three lengths of a standard stress questionnaire in Chinese heart patients who smoked, in a 2010 validation study. Stress can trigger smoking and relapse, so measuring it well matters for quit programmes.

Nearly two thousand patients from ten Hong Kong hospital clinics completed the survey. Analysis backed a two-part structure for all three versions, with positive and negative item groups pulling in opposite directions, and acceptable consistency within each part. Links with smoking habits and health measures also behaved as expected. Shorter versions held up well enough for busy clinic use.
europmc-pmc2954944:
Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien offered clearer guidance for scoping studies, a style of evidence review that maps a field rather than answering one narrow question, in a 2010 methods article. A widely used framework from 2005 left several steps vague.

From running three such studies themselves, they recommend tying each review's question tightly to its purpose and balancing breadth against what a team can finish. Study picking and data extraction should proceed in rounds with the whole team. Results need both counts and themes, plus thought about use, and asking stakeholders should be a required final step.
europmc-pmc2970544:
Ndimubanzi and colleagues systematically reviewed reports on neurocysticercosis, brain infection by pork tapeworm larvae, with special attention to people with epilepsy, in a 2010 study. Estimates of its frequency varied wildly worldwide.

Searching dozens of databases for studies from 1990 to mid-2008, they winnowed hundreds of papers down to a small set using brain imaging for diagnosis. Despite wide variation across groups, one figure held steady: roughly three in ten people with epilepsy in the pooled studies harboured the infection. Only one community survey measured its frequency in a whole village population.
europmc-pmc2993644:
Souza and the WHO survey group analysed caesarean births without medical indication in a 2010 study of the WHO Global Survey on Maternal and Perinatal Health. Sections chosen for non-medical reasons were under worldwide debate, and harms needed firmer numbers.

Records covered well over a quarter million deliveries in hundreds of facilities across twenty-four countries. About one percent of births were sections with no recorded indication. Compared with natural vaginal birth, every other delivery mode, including such sections, carried higher risk of death, intensive care admission, transfusion, or womb removal for the mother. The pattern strengthens caution about elective surgery.
europmc-pmc3019144:
Bozdagi and co-authors studied mice missing one copy of Shank3, a scaffolding gene at nerve junctions whose loss causes a deletion syndrome and autism in people, in a 2010 study. The gene recruits receptor and skeleton parts to the receiving side of synapses.

Heterozygous mice showed weaker miniature synaptic currents and altered plasticity in brain slices, plus sparser staining for one receptor type in a memory region. Behaviour tests found faults in social interaction and communication. Modelling the single-copy loss in mice ties the human syndrome's social features to measurable synaptic weakness, offering a test bed for treatments.
europmc-pmc3056144:
Labute presented in 2009 a computer method that fills in the hydrogen atoms missing from most macromolecule structures. Experiments usually locate only the heavy atoms of proteins and bound drugs, yet hydrogen positions decide how molecules bind and react. His program, Protonate3D, places hydrogens automatically while also trying flipped side chains, alternate shapes, and different charge states for each group.

Its scoring weighs crowding, electric forces, solvent effects, and the cost of each charge state at a given acidity. Tests on known structures suggest the placements are accurate. Getting hydrogens right matters for drug design, since a flipped group or a wrong charge can change a predicted binding completely. The tool was built to prepare structures for the modeling work that follows structure solving. It handles ligands and solvent molecules alongside the main chain.
europmc-pmc3069744:
Vonrhein and colleagues described in 2011 the autoPROC toolbox, software that automates the messy first stage of X ray crystal work. Real diffraction data rarely match the textbook ideal. Crystals split, beam centers drift, several lattices overlap, and headers carry wrong values, any of which can quietly ruin a dataset.

The paper walks through these common failure modes and the checks the toolbox applies to catch them. It tests beam center conventions against the images themselves, hunts for extra lattices across many frames, and keeps indexing consistent across sweeps of data. Automation calls established processing programs under the hood and flags trouble for the user. The goal is to rescue borderline datasets that manual processing might discard, and to make routine datasets boringly reliable. Synchrotron users with heavy data flows are the main audience.
europmc-pmc3087144:
Backes, Markham, Moorehead, Cordero, Nankervis, and Giannone reviewed in 2011 how preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy disorder affecting many organs, affects newborn babies. The illness is progressive, and often the only way to protect the mother is to deliver early. That rescue trades one risk for another, since early birth itself harms babies, not only the extremely early ones.

Babies born just a few weeks early, the late preterm group, make up about two thirds of all preterm births and face real risks of illness and death. The review covers how the disorder is diagnosed, how pregnancies are managed, and what outcomes late preterm infants face. It then weighs strategies to time delivery and support the fetus for the best joint outcome. The authors stress how incomplete the evidence guiding these decisions remains.
europmc-pmc3156644:
Christopher Mann and colleagues reviewed how muscle repair goes wrong and turns to scarring in a 2011 paper in Skeletal Muscle. Healthy repair after injury is a choreographed act among immune cells, muscle stem cells, and support cells, guided by local and body-wide signals. In chronic diseases such as muscular dystrophy, the choreography breaks down.

Inflammation refuses to switch off, support cells stay activated, and the stem cells that should rebuild fibres tire out. The end state is fibrosis, stiff scar tissue replacing working muscle, shared by nearly all long-running muscle diseases. The review gathers new findings on signals among stem cells, immune cells, fibroblasts, and the surrounding matrix, arguing muscle offers a model for wound healing across the body.
europmc-pmc3164644:
Taisei Kikuchi and colleagues sequenced the genome of a pine-killing nematode worm in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The worm causes a devastating pine wilt epidemic across Asia and Europe. It took up plant parasitism independently from other parasitic worms, while also feeding on fungi and hitching rides on insects. Its genome thus offers a fresh window on how parasitism evolves.

The worm carries the largest digestive enzyme set known in any nematode, plus expanded detox and transport families, suiting its varied foods and habitats. Its plant-wall softening proteins came not from worm ancestors but by gene transfer from fungi, and it lacks the weapon proteins of other plant parasites entirely. Gene-silencing machinery and stress systems are rich, while smell receptors are trimmed. The genome confirms a wholly separate route into plant parasitism.
europmc-pmc3169444:
Catrine Tudor-Locke and colleagues converted activity guidelines into step targets for older and less mobile adults in a 2011 paper. Step counters offer an easy way to track walking, but nobody had stated how many steps embody the official advice for these groups. The review pooled typical counts and intervention results.

Healthy older adults average a few thousand steps daily, and people with disability or chronic illness fewer still. Walking programmes added a modest daily rise in older adults and a larger one in special populations. Half an hour of brisk walking beyond daily routine lands near eight thousand steps on active days, within a broad whole-day band. Frailer groups may never reach brisk pace, the authors note, so targets must flex.
europmc-pmc3240744:
Cláudia Rosa-Ferreira and Sean Munro worked out how lysosomes hitch onto the motor that carries them outward in the cell, in this 2011 study in Developmental Cell. Lysosomes travel both ways along microtubule tracks, and a small switch protein called Arl8 was known to promote their movement. The team searched for what Arl8 grabs onto.

They found Arl8 binds a soluble protein called SKIP, previously known as a target of a Salmonella effector that hijacks the same motor for the bacterium's vacuole. In uninfected cells, both Arl8 and SKIP were required for lysosomes to spread away from the cell center. SKIP carries two docking motifs for the kinesin-1 motor's light chain; without them lysosomes fail to load the motor and stay put. A natural splice variant lacking one motif cannot drive movement, suggesting fine-tuning.
europmc-pmc3262844:
John Morris and colleagues built clusterMaker, a plugin that brings many clustering algorithms into the Cytoscape network platform, in this 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Biologists drowning in high-throughput data need to group similar items, genes, proteins, or samples, to see meaningful patterns, and to combine datasets from different experiments. Accessible tools for that were lacking.

The plugin implements a wide menu of algorithms, including hierarchical clustering, k-means, k-medoid, and several network-specific methods, some available to Cytoscape users nowhere else. Results appear as network views, dendrograms, and heat maps that stay linked: selecting items in one view highlights them everywhere. The authors demonstrate three uses, finding phenotype-specific mouse interaction networks, dissecting a yeast protein complex, and reannotating an enzyme family member. Session files for each scenario accompany the paper.
europmc-pmc3285644:
Michael Fehlings and colleagues reported the STASCIS trial, a multicenter study of surgical timing after cervical spinal cord injury, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Animal evidence strongly favors decompressing the cord early, but proof in patients was lacking. The prospective study enrolled adults with traumatic neck cord injuries at six North American centers and compared surgery within a day of injury against later surgery.

Of the patients with six-month follow-up, the early group fared better. About one in five had improved by at least two grades on the standard impairment scale. In the late group the share was roughly one in eleven. After adjusting for initial severity and steroid use, early surgery nearly tripled the odds of that improvement. Deaths were one in each group, and complication rates were similar, slightly favoring early surgery. The authors conclude early decompression is safe and improves recovery.
europmc-pmc3329544:
Ritchie and Romanuk combined trials to judge whether probiotics, foods and supplements carrying live helpful bacteria, really ease gut diseases, in a 2012 analysis. Separate reviews had praised probiotics for single conditions, but nobody had compared their value across diseases with very different causes. The team pooled randomized trials in people across eight gastrointestinal conditions.

Probiotics helped overall, cutting the risk of a poor outcome by roughly two fifths across the trials. Benefits were clear in six of the eight diseases, including pouchitis, infectious diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, and diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Traveler's diarrhea and a severe intestinal disease of premature babies showed no clear benefit. Most bacterial species helped, though three popular ones did not. The authors advise matching the disease and the bacterial strain carefully when choosing a probiotic.
europmc-pmc3400644:
Zhang and colleagues validated a shortened depression questionnaire in 2012 for people living with HIV in British Columbia, Canada. The standard scale runs twenty items; the short form keeps ten. Their test group was more than five hundred patients starting antiretroviral therapy in the provincial drug program.

Scores on the short form tracked the full scale almost perfectly. Its internal consistency was strong, and it classified patients with depressive symptoms nearly as accurately as the original, with high sensitivity and specificity. Analysis showed the short form kept the same two underlying themes, positive and negative feeling. The authors conclude the ten-item version is a sound, quicker stand-in for research with HIV-positive patients.
europmc-pmc3441244:
Marleau, Chen, Joyce, and Tullis proposed in 2012 that filtering cancer's messenger vesicles out of the blood could become a treatment in its own right. Tumors shed huge numbers of these exosomes, tiny sacs that carry growth proteins and immune-damping cargo to other cells. In HER2-driven breast cancer, vesicles bearing that growth protein even soak up the antibody drug meant to block it.

Drug strategies to block vesicle release or action carry toxicity and interaction risks. The authors instead describe a dialysis-like platform that traps vesicles on binding agents as blood circulates outside the body. A sibling device already cuts virus loads in hepatitis C patients, and viruses match exosomes in size and surface sugars. Removing the messengers, they argue, could restore immune attack.

Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862. It is Document 444 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consuls handled the practical edge of foreign policy: shipping, seamen, trade papers, and the protection of citizens abroad. Kreismann, a German-born Chicago editor, served the Union in the Prussian capital alongside Minister Judd. An instruction addressed to a consul rather than a minister points to business of that practical kind. Letters like this widen the picture of wartime diplomacy beyond courts and cabinets, down to the offices where Americans abroad actually got help.
frus-1862-d544:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 544 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Seward wrote as Lee's army crossed into Maryland and the government braced for the autumn crisis. His note to the Dutch minister kept the Washington end of the Netherlands file in order at a moment when larger matters pressed. The correspondence's subjects remained the standing ones of neutral trade and maritime right. There is a kind of reassurance in the file's regularity. Through the worst weeks of 1862, the letters between Seward and Van Limburg went back and forth like clockwork. The relationship they served never cracked.
frus-1862-d644:
On 27 November 1861 Townsend Harris wrote his last letter in this run of the Japanese file, addressed to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 644 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Four days after his previous dispatch, Harris wrote again from Edo, in the closing weeks of his mission. He would leave Japan the following spring. His health was broken by the post he had created. His final letters report the treaty system standing and the legation's affairs in order for his successor. The volume's Japanese strand thus ends where it began, with the first minister's own hand. It is a quiet, fitting close to the farthest-flung correspondence in the record of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d144:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 3 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 144 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the day wound up a set sent at the height of the ship question. Adams's April mail is among the most tense in the volume, as Britain weighed whether to let Southern warships sail. This letter ends the 3 April three. It is a working piece of the watch that, in the end, helped keep the British fleet out of the South's hands.
frus-1863p1-d244:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 23 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 244 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d344:
On 29 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 344 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d44:
On 13 December 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to Edwin De Leon. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; De Leon was a Southern agent working in Europe. The letter is document 44 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

De Leon served the South as a roving hand in Europe, where the work mixed talks, print, and quiet deals. Benjamin's letters to such men carried orders and cash-side news from home. This one came in mid-December, as the year of the South's best hopes closed. It is part of the group of Confederate papers printed in the Union's record, a rare chance to read the foe's mail.
frus-1863p1-d444:
A dispatch dated 4 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d544:
From Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 30 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d644:
The 23 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d144: Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to General Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, on November 20, 1943. The letter is Document 144 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Stimson-to-Marshall letters carried the War Department's mind on the great choices of the war, and this one was written two days before Cairo opened. The record gives the two men and the date. Its subject is in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d244:
The President's Log, the official booklet recording Roosevelt's trip to Africa and the Middle East in November and December 1943, is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The note exists to explain what the log is before its text is printed in the pages that follow.

The booklet runs to sixty-six numbered pages, with front and back matter and some fifty pages of pictures and appendices. Lieutenant William Rigdon prepared it, and Rear Admiral Wilson Brown approved it. Inside are the President's party list, an itinerary, sea and air travel charts, a foreword, and the log itself. Eleven appendices follow, from a citation for General Eisenhower to the Cairo and Tehran communiqués.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d344:
Alexander Kirk, the American minister in Egypt, wrote a short secret memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943 about his custody of the Cairo communiqué. It records a small errand at the center of the conference's secrecy.

That afternoon Harry Hopkins handed Kirk a copy of the communiqué on the Anglo-American-Chinese talks and asked him to hold it until instructions came from Tehran about its release. The timing was undecided, but Kirk would get twenty-four hours' notice so the three countries could publish at the same moment. Kirk was also to notify the Chinese legation when the word came. His own task, as he summed it up, was simply to see that American correspondents in Cairo received the text through the Office of War Information.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d44: Roosevelt also wrote to Churchill on October 14, 1943, making at least three summit letters in a single day. This one is Document 44 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The date fell in the final week of preparation for the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers. The record gives the parties and the date and leaves the contents to the text. It rests in the Foreign Relations volume with its companions of that busy day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d444:
Marked with a footnote in the printed volume, this second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes from December 5, 1943 covers another session of the joint American-British command at Cairo. The Second Cairo Conference was then deciding the next phase of the war against Germany and Japan. The State Department later published the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Session minutes preserve the order of business, the officers' exchanges, and the conclusions reached before the chiefs reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill. Having two records from one day shows how much was pressed into these meetings. For a reader tracing how Allied plans took final shape, that density is the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d544:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 11, 1944, keeping up the steady channel between the department and the White House. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, among the follow-up papers of the new year.

Hull's January traffic with Roosevelt mixed the conferences' unfinished business with the planning of the postwar order, a subject Hull cared about deeply. The Secretary had built his reputation on patient, formal diplomacy, the opposite of summit improvisation. For readers, the message shows the permanent government digesting the leaders' December decisions and fitting them into policy that could last.
frus-1944-quebec-d144:
Roosevelt replied to Churchill's Italian report the next day, August 30, 1944, in telegram 611. He was glad to hear how General Wilson had concentrated his forces and renewed the offensive. His own chiefs believed a vigorous attack, pressed with everything available, should force the enemy into the Po Valley.

The president stressed destroying German forces while they were within grasp, lest divisions escape to other fronts. He was confident Eisenhower would be satisfied that the Mediterranean effort was mauling troops that might otherwise face him. On the future use of Wilson's armies, Roosevelt suspended decision until the campaign's results were known. Trieste and Istria, he said, they would renew at Octagon, the Quebec meeting.
frus-1944-quebec-d244:
Hull asked Roosevelt for instructions on the French lend-lease agreement on September 11, 1944. The sticking point was Jean Monnet's request for industrial items to restart French production for the civil population. Under the July 15 memorandum Roosevelt had approved, such long-life industrial goods could go on credit only if necessary to the war in Europe or to forces just after an armistice.

Applied now, Hull wrote, that rule flatly rejected Monnet's program of over a billion dollars in industrial items. He recommended neither rejection nor approval. Instead, a list mechanism would leave the president complete discretion, item by item, as French behavior warranted. The Foreign Economic Administration would submit proposed French programs to Roosevelt before they joined the list.
frus-1944-quebec-d44:
September 1, 1944 opened with a Churchill message to Roosevelt. It was the first day of the conference month. The State Department placed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

September opened with Allied armies at the German frontier. The Quebec meeting stood eleven days away. Churchill's letters ran ahead of him across the Atlantic. They stated what Britain needed from the conference. For readers, the message marks a final approach. The Prime Minister was at sea or about to sail. The agenda for the meeting was effectively set. Only the arguments in person remained.
frus-1945-50-intel-d144:
Formal minutes cover the Second Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 26 March 1946. It survives in print as document 144 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d244:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee on 22 October 1947. The State Department prints it as document 244 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d344:
A memorandum dated 12 April 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It survives in print as document 344 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d44: A White House memorandum dated 7 November 1945 sits among the department papers of the intelligence volume. Papers from the president's house carry special weight in such a run. Since every department knew the final choice on a central intelligence system would be made there. The title gives no author, so the paper stands on its origin and date. Written while the Budget Bureau's plan was gaining ground in the autumn contest of 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d144:
Premier Mikolajczyk appealed straight to the President, and Ambassador Ciechanowski delivered the plea in Washington. The Polish ambassador's covering note, sent on 27 October 1944, passes on Mikolajczyk's telegram of the day before. Both texts are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Mikolajczyk protests the pressure on his government to accept the Curzon Line at once, without any reservations. All his work, he writes, has aimed at Polish-Soviet understanding, for Poland's sake and for the common cause. Yet his nation would feel terribly deceived, he warns, if this were the answer to its sacrifices and its unbroken part in the war. He asks the President for a reply and decisions at the earliest possible moment.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d244:
One China policy for three allies is the aim of this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. “Unity of Anglo-American-Soviet Policy Toward China” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It names the discords that could wreck the aim before they grow.

Some British elements, the paper warns, seem for imperial reasons to want a weak and possibly divided China after the war. A second fear runs the other way. Russia may use the Chinese Communists to carve out a separate area in the north or in Manchuria. The recommendation follows plainly. The United States should take the lead in helping China build a strong, stable, and unified government. Such a China could be the chief steadying force in the Far East. British and Russian help should be sought to that end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d344:
Bremen and Bremerhaven would stay under full American control, under an agreement the Combined Chiefs of Staff approved at Yalta in February 1945. The enclave, drawn on an attached map, covered the ports and their ground. American military government would run it, including disarmament and the breaking up of German war power there.

At the same time, the American commander was to follow the broad policies used in the British zone around it. He kept the right to depart from them on military grounds when he judged it needful. Transit rights each way — American stores southward, British movement toward Austria — complete the bargain.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d44: Roosevelt answered Churchill on 6 January 1945, the same day the prime minister's latest message arrived. His reply is document 44 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Same-day exchanges show the machinery at full stretch, with the president's staff turning cables around quickly because the Mediterranean journey was now only weeks away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d444:
A whole frontier might fall to Britain alone, and London disliked the prospect in this statement of February 10, 1945. If British proposals for occupation zones in Austria were approved, the entire Austro-Yugoslav frontier would be a British responsibility. Yugoslavia had not asked to alter the Styrian stretch. But it had advanced claims to Klagenfurt and parts of Carinthia, lost in the plebiscite of 1919.

Action might be needed to resist Yugoslav efforts to press those claims. Yugoslav partisans might also advance into Carinthia during operations and hold ground there. For Britain to stand alone in such a quarrel, the paper argues, would be invidious. The warning proved exact within months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d144:
British Minister John Balfour delivered London's draft agenda for the summit in a letter dated May 29, 1945. The letter is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had told Truman that his government was drawing up, at the President's wish, a list of subjects for the next meeting of heads of government.

Foreign Secretary Eden now asks Balfour to forward the enclosed list to Acting Secretary Grew, so the President can be informed. The list itself is printed with the next document. Balfour's short covering letter marks the moment the conference stopped being only about dates and houses. The British put their proposed business in writing. And the long argument over Poland, Germany, and the Balkans took paper form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d244:
Ambassador Winant reported the Foreign Office's protest in full in a second telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 244 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, and it tells the same story as the extract printed earlier in the volume.

An official named Harvey was considerably disturbed, Winant writes. And the British Embassy in Washington was told to ask for a postponement. The postponement would last until Italy's future status could be discussed at the Big Three meeting. London held that Italy's admission was tied to the peace treaty, and its Berlin delegation was fully briefed to discuss it there. With Churchill and Eden both away, the Foreign Office could not decide in the time given. The question would go to Eden, to raise with Byrnes, while London strongly urged delay.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d344:
Elmer Davis, who ran the Office of War Information, wrote to President Truman on July 4, 1945, with an idea to hold in mind at Berlin. His suggestion concerned action after the conference, not during it. The central problem of Germany, Davis argued, was the reeducation of the German people.

Without that change, he warned, every other measure would be a brief patch at best. The aim was a Germany no longer dangerous to its neighbors. Davis noted that the news service his office ran with the Army, through papers, radio, and newsreels, was already the real start of that teaching, whether planned or not.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d44:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Truman a personal and top secret telegram from London on May 31, 1945. It is document 44 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, sent as the Allied leaders arranged their first meeting since Germany's surrender. Churchill's own plans, he says, depend on the date Truman picks.

Churchill also raises a point of pride and fairness. He reports good talks with Truman's envoy Joseph Davies, but warns he will not attend a meeting that simply continues a private conference between Truman and Stalin. The three leaders, he insists, should meet at the same time and on equal terms. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman in person for the first time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d444:
American supervision of Greek elections is put to President Truman in a memorandum from the Secretary of State dated July 4, 1945. The question, it opens, raises an issue of the first importance. America has repeatedly affirmed President Roosevelt's purpose. He stated it in his State of the Union message of January 6, 1945. Peoples, Roosevelt said, have the right to choose the form of government under which they will live.

The memorandum adds a further obligation. The right of liberated peoples to choose their government must not be defeated by interim authorities holding power in the meantime. At the end of the paper stands the President's own manuscript endorsement: I agree, Harry S Truman. The decision was thus taken at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d544:
Secretary of State James Byrnes answered Secretary of War Stimson in a brief wire sent July 12, 1945. Byrnes was aboard the cruiser Augusta, sailing with President Truman to the Potsdam Conference. His reply is document 544 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the conference.

Byrnes says he has Stimson's wire and has talked it over with the President. The lend-lease question, he adds, is a complex one. He suggests the two men talk it over in person at Terminal, the code name for Potsdam. Editors note that a second reply went out the same day, and no one can now tell which was sent first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d644:
Ambassador Winant passed on British Foreign Office views on the Levant from London on July 9, 1945. His secret wire is document 644 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The remarks came from a Foreign Office official that day.

The official said France's offer to hand over the Troupes Speciales had come too late to help France. Made earlier, it might have bought a return favor. Syrians instead see it as only partial payment for the damage done to Damascus. The 45 days set to work out the transfer were called useful, since delay could cool tempers. As French elections neared, de Gaulle might grow more willing to compromise. On troop withdrawal, the official doubted any early move and preferred that a conference be put off.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1044:
British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden wrote to Secretary Byrnes from Berlin on July 23, 1945, about the coal directive for zone commanders in Germany. Both foreign offices had debated changes to the draft. Eden reports that London now agrees with the revised text handed over in Washington on July 11. A matching directive will go out at once to the British zone commander as an interim order.

Eden asks how Truman means to raise the directive with Stalin, at a plenary session or in private. He stresses that coal is among the most dangerous world shortages. Winning Russian support for the European Coal Organisation matters, he argues, since Polish support would likely follow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1144:
Staff of the British team at Potsdam drafted this memorandum on 18 July 1945, early in the talks. Each side used such papers to set out its case in full. A memorandum could be handed across, read aloud, or kept as the team's own record of its stand.

British papers of this kind put London's argument in London's words. The other teams then knew what to answer, and later readers know what was claimed. This one dates from the first week, when stands were still being staked out. It keeps the British view in its own phrasing, inside the American record of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1244:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 24 July 1945. Formal proposals were the bargaining chips of the summit. Each one claimed ground in writing and forced the other teams to answer in kind, amend, or refuse.

A paper from the second week came after the opening stands were known. The trades had begun, and drafts now aimed at terms the others might accept. This proposal is one such move. Kept in the official record, it shows what Washington put on the table at that point, in the exact words its team chose.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1344:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Winston Churchill on 24 July 1945, while both men led their delegations at Potsdam. The two had met in person only days before, at the start of the conference. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Letters between heads of government sit at the top of the diplomatic pile, above cables and staff papers. Even at a summit where the men could talk face to face, some things were still put in writing to make them firm. This exchange belongs to the last week of Churchill's wartime premiership. It ended while the conference was still sitting, giving the letter a place in two stories at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-144: Standing in the run of unnumbered pieces after document 710, this short note speaks for the editors of the Potsdam volume. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series exist to keep the archive legible. One might cite the file a paper came from. Another might point ahead to a later text. This note does that quiet work for its neighbors.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-44:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 20, 1945, catch the debate over liberated Europe in shorthand. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen records the foreign ministers' report being received, then the argument that followed.

A change in the Council of Foreign Ministers text was adopted, providing for a permanent secretariat. Discussion then turned to what the foreign secretaries favored for Bulgaria, Rumania, and Greece. Molotov indicated that present restrictions should be relaxed now that the war had ended. Churchill intervened on elections with a point of language and duty. Supervision of elections, he insisted, does not mean control, and Byrnes offered the softer word observation instead. Byrnes then proposed Italy's admission to the United Nations, paired with a declaration against admitting Spain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d744:
Document 744 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 25, 1945. It comes from the heart of the conference's second week. Staff drafted it to move a question forward inside the team. The paper was preserved and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Mid-conference drafts show ideas under pressure. Writers knew the other sides' lines by now. Readers can watch American drafting adjust to that knowledge. The document's value is its timing: late enough to be informed, early enough to still shape events. Such papers are the negotiation's true workshop floor.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d844:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Melbourne in Rumania on July 28, 1945, in document 844. Washington sent further guidance to its acting representative in Bucharest. The letter dates from the conference's last days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A second guidance letter in the same run shows a channel in heavy use. Melbourne's reports had built a file that demanded answers. Readers see the home office responding at matching pace. The document pairs with the July 28 letter to the same post in this volume. Together they show Washington steering Bucharest through the summit's closing turns.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d944: William Clayton sent this short memorandum to Edwin Pauley on July 28, 1945. It passes along a paper from the United States Group Control Council staff. That paper raises questions about the return of art objects looted during the war. Clayton says America might accept the first two recommendations in it. He asks Pauley's views on the third, which turns on replacement of art versus simple return. He hopes the two of them can send General Clay a joint memorandum on the subject.
