Mice without Sei1 grew and formed tumors much like normal mice. Their pancreases, though, worked poorly. The split result shows one gene can matter greatly in one organ and little elsewhere. That nuance guides how Sei1 should be judged as a cancer target.
plos-pone-0008844:
Sascha Pust, Anne Berit Dyve, Maria Torgersen, and colleagues checked whether raft proteins guide toxins through cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flotillins sit in fatty patches of cell membranes and inner compartments. Two toxins offered test cargo: bacterial Shiga toxin and a plant toxin. Toxins hijack normal transport routes to reach their targets. Whether flotillins help or hinder that ride was open.

Altering flotillin levels changed how the toxins were taken up and moved. Transport and flotillin placement influenced each other. The interplay reveals a route toxins exploit inside cells. Blocking such routes could blunt toxin damage.
plos-pone-0008944:
Jianhua Ruan reported a winning entry to a gene-prediction contest in PLOS ONE in 2010. The contest, called DREAM3, asked teams to predict gene activity from data. Systems biologists build computer models of how genes turn each other up and down. Judging those models fairly is hard, so the contest used hidden test data.

Ruan's algorithm ranked among the top performers at predicting expression patterns. The paper explains the method and how it handled the challenge data. Contests like DREAM give the field a rare honest scoreboard for its tools. Strong prediction methods help researchers guess which genes drive a cell's behaviour.
plos-pone-0009044:
Hendrik Weisser and co-authors tested whether a virus's predicted vigour helps forecast HIV therapy results, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A virus's replicative capacity is how well it copies itself in the lab. Clinicians sometimes blame odd treatment responses on a strain's fitness. But its true value for predicting outcomes was murky.

The team predicted replicative capacity straight from the virus's genes. They used support vector machines, a pattern-finding algorithm. Adding that prediction barely improved forecasts of therapy response. The modest result tempers hopes that viral fitness numbers guide treatment much.
plos-pone-0009144:
Haiyan Huang and Qiang Wu catalogued the full detox gene family of the zebrafish, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ugt enzymes tag oily small molecules with a sugar acid to disarm them. Tagged molecules dissolve in water and can leave the body easily. This detox system handles many drugs and body wastes alike.

The team identified the complete Ugt set carried by the zebrafish. Comparing it with other species revealed the family's deep evolutionary variety. Fish carry their own expansions and losses of these detox genes. The catalogue supports using zebrafish to test how drugs break down.
plos-pone-0009244:
George Mtove and co-authors published this child health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Invasive salmonella infections are a serious danger to African children. Yet hard numbers on how often they strike were scarce. The team ran fever surveillance at a rural hospital in Tanzania.

They tested children admitted with fever to estimate what share had invasive salmonellosis. They also compared their figures with earlier studies from other places. Reliable local numbers matter because treatment and vaccines depend on knowing the true burden. The study adds a rural Tanzanian measure to a map that is still mostly blank.
plos-pone-0009344:
Carina Banning and co-authors published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins constantly meet and part inside living cells, and those meetings run the cell. A technique called FRET can detect such meetings under a microscope. But microscopy is fiddly and can only survey a few cells at a time.

The team built a FRET assay that runs on a flow cytometer instead. Flow machines stream thousands of cells past a laser, reading each one. Their assay can therefore identify and analyze protein interactions in large cell numbers. That scale turns interaction hunting from a craft into a screen.
plos-pone-0009444:
Marietta Keckeis and co-authors compared sleep disorders and blood sugar in PLOS ONE in 2010. Past work had linked short or broken sleep with poor handling of sugar. Yet no study had set the main sleep disorders side by side to compare them. The team measured how patients handled glucose, the main sugar in blood.

Patients with sleep disorders showed impaired glucose tolerance more often than expected. The pattern linked disturbed nights to a step toward diabetes. Clinics that treat sleep may thus be a place to catch sugar problems early. The authors argue that fixing sleep could also help protect against diabetes.
plos-pone-0009544:
David Silvestre and colleagues found a second job for a known protein in tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most biologists know c-Fos as a gene switch in the cell nucleus. It can also sit at inner membranes and switch on fat molecule making. The team checked brain tumors from patients and from mice prone to such tumors. They looked at where c-Fos sat and what it was doing.

In these tumors, c-Fos in the cytoplasm was busy driving fat production. That activity helped tumors of both the central and peripheral nervous systems grow. A protein with a hidden second job offers a fresh target. Blocking that job might starve tumors of the fats they need.
plos-pone-0009644:
Nuria Pescador and co-authors studied fuel storage under low oxygen in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells store sugar as glycogen, a starch like reserve. When oxygen is scarce, cells lean more on stored fuel. The team asked how that stockpile gets built. The oxygen sensor HIF was the prime suspect, and an enzyme called glycogen synthase 1 does the building.

They showed that HIF drives production of glycogen synthase 1. With more of the enzyme, cells accumulated glycogen under low oxygen. The pathway explains a survival strategy for tissues starved of air. It may also matter in tumors, which grow in low oxygen pockets and hoard fuel.
plos-pone-0009844:
Genomes grow and change over deep time, yet they may all carry the same statistical fingerprints. Hong-Da Chen and colleagues searched for such universal imprints across genomes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Two measures anchor the claim: equivalent length and cumulative mutation density. Mutation density counts how many changes a stretch of DNA holds. Both measures describe how mutations pile up as genomes evolve. Finding the same pattern everywhere would mean genome growth follows shared rules. Rules like those help scientists compare evolution across all life. The imprints are called universal because they cross species lines.
plos-pone-0009944:
Building a ribosome, the cell's protein factory, takes helper enzymes that spend energy. Baskaran Anand, Parag Surana, and Balaji Prakash took apart one such helper's machinery. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 30S is the small subunit of the bacterial ribosome.

The helper is YqeH, a GTPase that aids assembly of the 30S ribosome subunit. GTPases burn the fuel molecule GTP to power their work. Deciphering the catalytic machinery means finding the parts that do the chemical work. Assembly helpers are possible targets for new antibiotics. Ribosomes are built, not born whole.
plos-pone-0010044:
The authors were Srinivasulu Chigurupati, Mohamed Mughal, Sic Chan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a wound treatment in mice. Healing skin wounds involves skin cells plus immune cells that move in. Too much oxidative stress and swelling can slow that repair, while antioxidants have been reported to help.

The team made a synthetic compound modeled on uric acid, a natural body chemical. In mice, that compound sped up healing of skin wounds. A faster-healing treatment could matter for chronic wounds that resist standard care, though mouse results need human testing.
plos-pone-0010144:
Jiang Zhu and co-workers reported a surprise about the smallest introns in a 2010 paper. The other authors were Fuhong He and Dapeng Wang. Introns are RNA stretches cut out before a gene message matures. Their removal is closely tied to how messages leave the cell nucleus for the cytosol.

Many vertebrate introns have a minimal size near one hundred DNA letters. The team found a novel role for these minimal introns in routing messages outward. A routing job for such tiny introns changes how biologists think about gene layout and message handling.
plos-pone-0010244:
Sakshi Puri and Zen Faulkes asked whether shrimp-like animals sense harmful acid in 2010. Nociception is the body's detection of damaging stimuli, a sense expected across animal groups. It should trigger strong, reliable behavior when an animal meets something harmful. Yet in invertebrates like crustaceans, this sense is poorly studied compared with vertebrates.

The pair tested decapod crustaceans, the group with crabs, shrimp, and lobsters. They asked whether these animals have nociceptors, dedicated sensors, for extreme pH. Their PLOS ONE study adds evidence to debates about pain-like responses in invertebrate animals.
plos-pone-0010344:
Jeannie Te, Igor Dozmorov, Joel Guthridge and a large group hunted for blood markers of lupus kidney disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lupus can inflame the kidneys, a complication called lupus nephritis. Tiny RNA pieces called microRNAs help control gene activity. The team wondered whether a distinct set of them shows up when kidneys are involved. They used chip tests to compare microRNA levels in blood cells.

Samples came from patients, and the chips scanned many microRNAs at once. A unique pattern stood out for those with kidney disease. Such a pattern could one day help doctors spot kidney trouble without a biopsy. It might also reveal which gene controls go wrong in this complication. First, though, the signature gives researchers a concrete lead to verify.
plos-pone-0010444:
Beth Kochin, Andrew Yates, Jacobus de Roode and colleagues modeled what stops early malaria in rodents for PLOS ONE in 2010. When malaria parasites first surge in the blood, something halts their rise. Three candidates compete: tailored immunity, general innate immunity, or simply running low on red blood cells to infect. Mice lacking tailored immunity show the same early pattern as normal mice. That fact already weakens the first candidate.

The authors used math models to test the remaining explanations against data. Pinpointing the brake matters for vaccines, which try to add brakes of their own. If red cell supply is the real limit, vaccine logic changes. Rodent malaria is a stand-in for the human disease, with limits. Still, the study sharpens a basic question in infection biology.
plos-pone-0010544:
Claudio Tennie, Josep Call and Michael Tomasello tested whether chimpanzees copy goals rather than exact motions in PLOS ONE in 2010. How apes learn hard skills from each other is still debated. Two mechanisms lead the debate: imitation of actions, and emulation of results. Earlier studies rarely controlled the social setting well. The team used a floating peanut task, where a peanut must be moved through a tube, in social groups.

Chimps appeared to use emulation, learning the outcome to aim for without copying each move. That distinction matters for theories of culture in animals. Emulation spreads goals fast but may lose fine technique. Controlled social tests are hard with apes, making this evidence valuable. The study refines what chimpanzee culture can and cannot transmit.
plos-pone-0010644:
Ryota Satoh and colleagues asked how the fly sense of smell keeps its signal clean, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Smell signals pass from the antenna into a brain area called the antennal lobe. There, the signal could easily blur or lose detail.

Combining recordings with a network model, the team found the lobe preserves as much information as possible. Local circuits sharpened some inputs and trimmed noise. The design matches a principle proposed for other senses too. A brain that wastes nothing gives engineers a useful template for building artificial noses and sensors.
plos-pone-0010744:
Andres Zuluaga and colleagues tested whether generic gentamicin works as well as the brand product, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulators approve generic injectable antibiotics largely on chemical sameness. Reports of deaths tied to other generic drugs had raised doubts about that shortcut.

Mice with low white cell counts received thigh infections, then brand or generic versions. The products did not all perform alike against the infection. Some generics killed fewer bacteria at the same dose. Results like these argue for live testing of critical generics, since paper sameness does not guarantee equal cure.
plos-pone-0010844:
Ya-Hui Wang, Jean-Pierre Gorvel, Yen-Ting Chu and colleagues published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicobacter pylori is the bacterium behind many cases of stomach inflammation, ulcers, and stomach cancer. It is usually thought to live outside cells, yet the team found it copying itself inside mouse dendritic cells, the scouts that alert the immune system.

Inside those cells, the bacteria sat in compartments tied to the cell's recycling system, and bacterial counts rose sharply within hours. Infection trapped key display molecules inside, blocking their move to the cell surface where they would flag danger for other immune cells. Even killed bacteria kept this blocking effect, linked to signals from the bacterial outer coat. Wang and colleagues show one way this germ can blunt the very response meant to clear it.
plos-pone-0010944:
Audrun Utskarpen, Ramiro Massol, Bo van Deurs and co-authors published this toxin study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Shiga toxin, made by certain E. coli, enters cells mainly through clathrin-coated pits, little cradles that pinch off pieces of the cell surface. The toxin also switches on a signaling enzyme, Syk, and the team asked how that signal changes the entry machinery.

Under the electron microscope, brief toxin treatment increased the number of coated pits at the cell surface, and live imaging showed more of the pits' adapter protein gathered there too. Both effects vanished when Syk could not work. Utskarpen and colleagues show the toxin does not just use the cell's doors; it orders more doors built. That insight may suggest ways to block entry of a toxin behind severe foodborne disease.
plos-pone-0011044:
Michael Cox, Martin Allgaier, Byron Taylor and co-authors published this cystic fibrosis microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. CF airways host bacterial communities shaped by age, treatment, and lung damage, but how those communities differ between young and old patients was rudimentary. Using a phylogenetic microarray that identifies bacteria by their DNA, the team profiled airways across the lifespan.

Their stable patients ranged from infants under a year old to adults in their seventies. Older patients with poorer lung function carried more uneven communities, dominated by fewer, related groups, while samples followed over time showed young patients' communities diversifying early and older patients losing diversity. Cox and colleagues chart a lifelong ecological succession in the CF lung. Knowing its normal course helps doctors judge when a community shift signals danger.
plos-pone-0011144:
Yewdall, Drutman, Jinwala and colleagues dissected a vaccine step in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vaccines based on dendritic cells aim to train killer T cells against targets like cancer. The team found these vaccine cells cannot start that training entirely on their own.

Instead, they must hand their antigen cargo to the body's own presenting cells first. That handoff is required before killer T cells get primed. Missing this step may explain why some cell vaccines underperform in patients. Designing vaccines to ensure the handoff could make cancer vaccines work better.
plos-pone-0011244:
Shulman, Chibnik, Aubin and colleagues searched for Alzheimer pathways in PLOS ONE in 2010. Instead of treating the disease as one uniform process, they used measurable traits that sit between genes and symptoms. Those middle traits can reveal separate routes that all end in the same diagnosis.

The analysis identified divergent pathways toward Alzheimer disease. Different routes suggest different treatments may suit different patients. Matching drugs to the pathway a patient follows could succeed where single drugs for all have failed. The study supports a more precise approach to a disease that has resisted simple solutions.
plos-pone-0011344:
Lutz Bornmann and Hans-Dieter Daniel asked in 2010 whether peer review does a good job of picking which papers a journal should publish. Journals rely on expert reviewers to judge submitted work, and later citations are often used to grade whether those judgments were right. The authors warned that a strong link between reviewer scores and later citations alone does not prove review is worth its cost.

They carried out a utility analysis using a high-impact journal as their case. Their approach weighed what review gains against what it costs in time, effort, and missed good papers. The study gives editors a stricter way to judge their own gatekeeping. It also reminds researchers that review is a tool with limits, useful only when its benefits clearly beat the burden it places on science.
plos-pone-0011444:
Anup Kumar Nair and co-authors ran a case-control study in 2010 on gene variants and type 2 diabetes in South India. Diabetes strikes South Indians at high rates and at younger ages than in many populations. The team tested variants in three genes tied to glucose handling and vitamin A transport, comparing patients with healthy controls from the same population.

Variants in the STRA6 gene showed a clear association with the disease in this group, while the other genes did not carry the same signal. An India-specific clue matters because most diabetes genetics came from European samples whose findings do not always transfer. The result adds STRA6 to the list of genes deserving deeper study in South Asian diabetes. It also supports building genetic knowledge population by population rather than assuming one map fits all.
plos-pone-0011544:
Christopher Rhea, Shirley Rietdyk, and Jeffery Haddad staged a contest in 2010 between two ways the body adapts when vision lies. Volunteers stepped over an obstacle that an illusion made look taller than it was. With practice, either perception recalibrates, so the ledge looks its true height, or the stepping movement recalibrates, lifting the foot by the right amount while the ledge still looks tall.

Their experiments reveal which system adjusts when the eyes misreport an obstacle, movement or perception, and how fast each learns. The answer matters beyond the lab, since falls in older adults often involve misjudged curbs and steps. Knowing whether training should target seeing or stepping guides better prevention. The study is a clean example of the brain keeping two ledgers for the same fact, and updating only one of them.
plos-pone-0011644:
Claire Cole and co-authors tested lab-made sugar fragments against blood vessel growth, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heparan sulfate, a natural sugar chain, helps organise signals that tell vessels to grow. Tumours exploit that growth to feed themselves, a process called angiogenesis, so blocking it is a long-standing cancer strategy.

The team built precise synthetic versions of these sugars and applied them to endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. The fragments inhibited cell functions that vessel growth requires. Defined sugar decoys like these could become a new class of anti-angiogenesis agents, with structures tuned exactly rather than drawn from natural mixtures.
plos-pone-0011744:
Lifan Luo and co-authors scanned tiny gene-tuning RNAs in pig testes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These short RNAs, called microRNAs, are known to help steer sperm growth in mammals. Their levels and jobs in pig germ cells, though, were not fully known.

With a chip holding probes for more than a thousand microRNAs, the team compared young, immature testes with mature ones. They found microRNAs whose levels shift as the testes mature. Those shifting tuners are prime suspects in the control of male fertility in farm stock, with worth for pig breeding programmes as well as basic reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0011844:
John Hunter and colleagues used a math model in 2010 to explain a small extra bump found on some human molars, the Carabelli cusp. Their starting point was the patterning cascade model, in which signals from small zones in the growing tooth shape the cusps that follow. Shape and gene activity feed back on each other as the tooth forms.

The model predicts whether the Carabelli cusp appears, how large it grows, and whether it shows the same form on both sides of the mouth. Matching those forecasts against real teeth tests whether a few simple rules can generate the variety dentists and anthropologists record. If the rules hold, tooth shape becomes a readable record of the growth process behind it.
plos-pone-0011944:
Chia-Lin Hsu, Colleen Neilsen, and Paul Bryce reported in 2010 that mast cells both make and answer to a key allergy signal. IL-33 is a recently described member of the IL-1 signal family, found in diseases such as severe asthma and inflammatory bowel disease. Added IL-33 was known to boost allergy-type immune responses and mast cell growth.

The team showed that mast cells themselves produce IL-33, and that the signal regulates inflammation that depends on IgE, the antibody class behind most allergies. A cell type manufacturing its own amplifier creates a feedback loop worth interrupting. That loop offers a defined target for calming allergic inflammation at its source.
plos-pone-0012044:
Thierry Poynard and co-workers asked in 2010 whether a famous researcher's conclusions last longer than an unknown's. The Hirsch index, or h-index, scores a scientist's output and influence, and it shapes hiring and funding. The team hypothesized that papers whose first author had a higher h-index would see their conclusions survive longer as truth.

Testing that idea in clinical research connects two uncomfortable questions: how science rewards fame, and how long medical truths endure. If prestige predicts survival of conclusions, peer review may be trusting names more than data. If it does not, the h-index's use as a quality stamp looks even weaker.
plos-pone-0012144:
Richarda de Voer, Liesbeth Mollema, Rutger Schepp, and co-authors measured meningitis vaccine protection across the Dutch population in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Netherlands had added a vaccine against meningococcal C disease in 2002, given to toddlers, with a catch-up drive for everyone up to eighteen. Years later, the team checked blood samples to see how immunity stood before and after that program.

Population blood surveys show whether a vaccine's protection lasts and how widely it spread, beyond what case counts alone can say. Their measurements give Dutch health officials a firm read on the program's reach. Results like these decide whether booster shots are needed and help other countries plan their own vaccine rollouts.
plos-pone-0012244:
David Smith, Stephen Smith, Celeste de Jager, and co-authors tested B vitamins against brain shrinkage in older people, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brains shrink faster in people with mild memory impairment, and a blood marker called homocysteine predicts that faster shrinkage. B vitamins lower homocysteine, so the team ran a randomized trial in people with mild cognitive impairment to see if lowering it slows the loss.

Scans showed the vitamin treatment did slow the accelerated shrinkage in these patients. Slowing brain loss in the mild stage is exactly where dementia prevention must act, before damage becomes permanent. A safe, cheap vitamin regimen with scan-proven effect is a rare bright result in this field, worth the larger trials it invites.
plos-pone-0012344:
Eszter Schoell, Ulrike Bingel, Falk Eippert and colleagues used brain scans in a 2010 PLOS ONE study to ask how the brain handles heat pain when its own opioid system is blocked. The body makes its own opioid chemicals, and they calm pain during stress and even during fake treatments that people believe in. Blocking their receptors lets researchers see what those chemicals normally do.

Volunteers felt heat on the skin while a drug blocked opioid receptors, and the team watched which brain areas changed their activity. The scans show that the opioid system shapes pain signals early, not just at the final feeling stage. That insight helps explain why opioid drugs work and why blocking them can undo pain relief from placebos.
plos-pone-0012444:
Andrew Pershing, Line Christensen, Nicholas Record and colleagues calculated what whaling did to the ocean carbon cycle, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. People have cut whales, big fish, and sharks to a small share of their former numbers. Big animals store carbon in their bodies and feed surface life whose waste sinks, so losing them may have weakened a natural carbon pump.

Their estimates suggest that restoring large whale populations would lock away notable amounts of carbon. Bigger, in this case, really was better for the climate system. The argument adds a climate reason, beyond ethics and ecology, to rebuild whale numbers that whaling erased.
plos-pone-0012544:
Mingshan Xue, Timothy Craig, Ok-Ho Shin and colleagues compared two look-alike trigger proteins in nerve cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Synaptotagmins release cell cargo when calcium floods in, using their paired C2 domains as calcium sensors. Family members 1 and 7 both sense calcium yet serve different release jobs, one fast and one slow.

Through structural and mutational analysis, the team pinned down what sets the two apart. Small changes in the sensor domains tune speed and grip. Knowing the tuning rules explains how cells run fast signaling and slow secretion side by side, and informs work on diseases of release, from diabetes to brain disorders.
plos-pone-0012644:
Tang, Jaganath and Sekaran tested plant extracts from the Phyllanthus group against human cancer cells. Plants in this group have a long history in folk care for liver disease, diabetes and other ills. Their 2010 study used water and alcohol extracts of four species on prostate cancer and skin cancer cells.

The extracts slowed the growth of those cancer cells while sparing normal cells more. They acted by pausing the cell cycle and pushing cancer cells into programmed death. Such results do not make a drug, but they mark the plants as worth deeper testing.
plos-pone-0012744:
Bailey, Brewer, Hendrixson and co-authors retested the family tree of trapdoor spiders in the genus Myrmekiaphila. A 2007 revision had set the genus at eleven species in three groups. Their 2010 study combined body traits with DNA to check that scheme in a single analysis.

Trapdoor spiders live hidden lives in burrows, so their true diversity is easy to miss. An integrated test can confirm species or expose hidden ones lumped under one name. Getting the tree right guides conservation for these little-known burrowing spiders.  The authors weigh both lines of evidence before naming groups.
plos-pone-0012844:
Schulz, Frechero, Appignanesi and co-authors explained how a slightly rough surface keeps soluble proteins watertight. A working protein must shield its internal backbone hydrogen bonds from water, or its structure falls apart. Proteins often bury those bonds or wrap other structures around them.

Their 2010 study shows sub-nanoscale ruggedness itself can seal exposed regions against water. A rule based on surface texture adds to the physics of protein folding. It may help designers build stable proteins for medicine and industry.  The authors measured ruggedness on structures solved by other groups.
plos-pone-0330144:
Gaganpreet K Gill and Dion G Durnford found hidden variety inside a flask of identical algae. A lab culture of a single-celled green alga, all cells genetically the same, split into light and dense layers when spun through a gradient. The two groups differed in size, protein, green pigment, and how well they photosynthesised, despite sharing one genome and one flask.

Under harsh bright light, the dense group resisted damage better, shed excess energy more capably, and barely bothered to adjust, as if already dressed for glare. It also shrugged off a chemical that mimics light stress. The authors propose a bet-hedging strategy: even a uniform population keeps a pre-armed minority ready for bad conditions, a cheap insurance policy written into single cells.
plos-pone-0336744:
Yeaeun Kim and co-authors tracked how often older South Koreans from outside the capital region are treated in Seoul-area hospitals. Using national discharge survey data, their 2026 study compared the years just before COVID-19 with the first pandemic years. The sample covered millions of weighted records for patients over sixty-five.

The overall share treated in the capital stayed the same, at about one in thirteen patients, across both periods. Under the surface, patterns shifted by age group and diagnosis. During the pandemic, patients with cancer, more severe illness, or surgery planned were more likely to travel to capital hospitals. Kim and colleagues argue regional hospitals need investment and clear plans to win back local patients.
plos-pone-0340244:
Damla Kaptan, Hannes Schroeder, Hege Ingjerd Hollund, and co-authors combined microscopy with DNA analysis to learn which microbes eat away at buried human bones. They studied medieval skeletons from cemeteries in southwestern Norway, comparing visible bone erosion with the microbial communities sequenced from the same bones and with burial conditions.

Well-preserved bones, especially those buried beneath church floors, hosted richer and more even microbial communities than heavily eroded bones from outdoor graves. One bacterial genus, Streptomyces, dominated and is a prime suspect in the decay. Fungi left clear traces under the microscope yet appeared in the DNA data only once, leaving their role unresolved. The authors show preservation and microbiome composition are tightly linked.
plos-pone-0340344:
Mansoorullah Muradi, Lima Oria, and Tariq Aziz Azizi compared what university students in Afghanistan, the Netherlands, and Turkey know and think about e-cigarettes. Vaping spread fast among young adults on a reputation for safety that evidence does not fully support. Their 2026 online survey asked students about use, knowledge, attitudes, and the habits of people around them.

More than half the students reported vaping, and use clustered where close friends or family smoked. Knowledge was weak overall, with over half showing poor understanding of health risks and rules. Most students voiced concern about vaping, yet nearly two thirds saw it as more socially acceptable than smoking. Tobacco smokers often vaped too, suggesting dual use rather than quitting. The authors call for education that corrects safety myths.
plos-pone-0341344:
Raouf Hammami and colleagues checked whether one-leg hop testing gives a trustworthy measure of leg imbalance in young soccer players. Coaches use the difference between a player's left and right hop distance to flag injury risk, but a measure that wobbles between days misleads. Sixty-four boys aged eight to sixteen, split by maturity, hopped for maximal distance on each leg in repeated sessions.

The imbalance scores showed good consistency across repeated testing, and the authors weighed how small a change the test can honestly detect at each maturity stage. That sensitivity question matters: a wobble within normal noise should not bench a child. With reliability mapped before and after puberty, academy staff can treat hop asymmetry as a usable monitoring number rather than a one-day snapshot, provided they respect its error margins.
plos-pone-0342144:
Grace Lemmon, Jaclyn M Jensen, Goran Kuljanin, and Mounica Reddy surveyed more than a thousand larger-bodied employees, plus several hundred of their coworkers, to map where weight-based mistreatment at work comes from. Their 2026 exploratory study combined the survey with national data on each respondent's occupation, testing four lenses: stereotypes, suppressed prejudice, objectification, and job context.

Mistreatment clustered where workplace talk prized thinness and where nobody pushed back against negative body talk, and in generally hostile interpersonal climates. Employees who felt they did not measure up to peers also reported more abuse. The pattern points in three directions at once: culture, coworkers, and self-image all feed the problem, so fixes aimed at only one will likely disappoint.
plos-pone-0343544:
Some microbes make special molecules that grab iron from their surroundings. Without iron, they cannot survive. Alejandro García Ríos and co-authors searched for these grabbers, called siderophores, inside three kinds of sea sponges. Their study appeared in PLOS One in 2026. They skipped growing microbes in dishes. Instead, they scanned sponge extracts with a precise chemical instrument.

Software then matched the signals against known iron-bound patterns. The search found fifty-nine candidate molecules. Several were already known from fungi and bacteria. Adding iron during extraction changed very little. That hints the sponge microbes produce these grabbers all the time. The matches still need proof from pure reference chemicals.
plos-pone-0345444:
Yanfang Liu and three colleagues build a system for predicting infrastructure disruption in New York City in this 2026 study. Urban supply chains depend on networks of roads and facilities whose failure cascades quickly. Their framework combines network analysis, a graph-based neural network that learns from the city's structure itself, and stress testing. It was trained on thousands of infrastructure nodes, nearly one hundred thousand recorded disruption events, and a large traffic flow archive.

The graph model predicted flow disruption far more accurately than four established forecasting baselines, and removing the network structure inflated its errors by nearly a third, proving the map itself carries information. Stress tests showed targeted attacks on hub nodes fragment the network fast, though random failures overtake them in total damage beyond a point. Past flow patterns and timing carried most of the predictive weight. The authors flag dual-risk nodes for priority protection.
plos-pone-0345644:
Yalda Hashempour and her team traced how long COVID-19 germs last in wards. They paired a scan of past work with tests in two wards in the north of Iran. They took swabs of air, tops, and waste water from COVID wards. Each swab was checked for the genes of the virus.

Traces showed in one fifth of air tests. They showed in one fourth of top tests. In waste water they showed in near two thirds. The team warns that gene traces are not proof of live germs. Still, the map shows where germs pool and where clean-ups must bite.
plos-pone-0347344:
Sara Karim and colleagues built SEEnet, a lightweight learning system that warns small satellites about radiation hits before they corrupt onboard data. Cheap nanosatellites fly off-the-shelf electronics that cosmic radiation easily upsets. Their framework pools several decision-tree classifiers of different depths into a voting ensemble, tuned to run in real time on feeble satellite hardware.

Trained on a public dataset from a German university's satellite program, SEEnet classified radiation events with seventy-seven percent accuracy, beating gradient boosting, random forests, and support vector machines in head-to-head tests. It also reports how confident each prediction is. The authors pitch it as an early-warning layer for low-cost missions.
plos-pone-0347544:
Danya Bakhbakhi and colleagues interviewed forty parents and family members in the United Kingdom who had lived through a stillbirth, asking which outcomes of care mattered most to them. The goal was to build a core outcome set, the minimum list every stillbirth study should report, grounded in families' priorities rather than researchers' habits. Interviews were analyzed with a grounded theory approach.

Families named three hundred forty-nine outcomes, and nearly nine in ten had never been reported in earlier stillbirth care studies. They grouped into clinical care, mental health and well-being, social and family life, and future pregnancies. The huge unreported share shows how much research has measured what was convenient instead of what bereaved parents needed to know.
plos-pone-0347644:
Manabu Tanimura, Kazuhiko Koike, and Kazumi Matsuoka study what Pacific oysters can digest. Their marine study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Oysters carry their own enzymes for breaking down plant fiber. That hints they might feed on land plant matter washed to sea. But holding an enzyme is not proof of eating the food.

The team fed one group algae and one group land leaves. They then compared gene activity in the two groups. The fiber enzymes held at a steady baseline in both. Fat-burning genes rose instead on the algae diet. The oyster seems to keep a standing toolkit for land food. Most of its fuel, though, comes from the sea.
plos-pone-0347744:
Li Wen and colleagues evaluated the quality and layout of higher education across China in a 2026 study. Yearbook data from 2000 to 2022 for all thirty-one provincial regions fed an index blending education with economic, social, and cultural development. Mapping tools then traced how the balance shifted across regions over two decades.

A statistical model probed what drives regional differences. Quality clustered unevenly, with some provinces concentrating strong universities while others lag. Seeing the geography of quality helps national planners decide where new investment narrows gaps rather than widening them. The long panel also shows whether past policies actually moved the balance.
plos-pone-0348344:
Saif-alnasr H. Mohammed and colleagues tested whether testosterone can quickly relax the uterus in rats. The hormone is known for slow, gene-driven effects, but hints existed of a fast action that could matter for conditions of excessive uterine contraction. Their 2026 study gave single injections to non-pregnant and late-pregnant rats and measured contractions with implanted sensors over hours.

Higher doses relaxed the uterus in a dose-dependent way, in both pregnant and non-pregnant animals, and the effect survived blocking the usual testosterone receptor, pointing to a fast, non-standard pathway involving calcium. Blood levels matched the doses given. The authors suggest testosterone-like compounds deserve study for uterine overactivity disorders.
plos-pone-0348444:
Amir Akerman and colleagues pinned down how a plant signalling protein called ROP10 sticks to the cell membrane and does its job. These switch proteins steer plant cell shape and growth, and one family branch lacks the usual fatty anchor, raising the question of what holds them in place. Using microscopy, biochemistry, and chemical analysis in the model plant Arabidopsis, the 2026 study tested candidate attachment points.

The protein indeed carries fatty acid tags on specific cysteine sites, confirmed directly by mass analysis, and one site proved essential for its membrane grip and for controlling cell polarity. Curiously, the permanently active form clung less tightly than the normal protein, the reverse of its cousins. The findings rewrite how this protein family partitions the membrane.
plos-pone-0349044:
XueYin Xu and co-authors priced a new two-drug combination for advanced liver cancer against the standard older drug, asking whether the extra benefit is worth the extra money in China. Their model followed patients through ten years of treatment, weighing drug and care costs against years lived in good health. The model used results from a large late-stage trial. Its yardstick was a willingness-to-pay line set at three times national income per person.

The combination's cost per healthy year came in far above that line, at roughly nearly three times the threshold. The chance it counted as good value at that price was effectively zero. Drug prices and quality-of-life values drove the result most. The authors do not dispute that the therapy can help patients; they conclude that at current prices it fails China's cost-effectiveness test, pointing negotiators toward price cuts.
plos-pone-0349144:
Wen Wei Chung and colleagues interviewed people living with HIV and the doctors and nurses who treat them in Malaysia about using a phone app for HIV self-care. Seventeen patients and eleven clinicians at a hospital infectious disease clinic shared what they would want, what worried them, and what would help. Interviews continued until no new themes appeared.

Patients saw the app as a route to knowledge, easier clinic visits, medicine refills, and direct contact with their care team. Concerns included information overload and privacy. Clinicians weighed the same benefits against workload and safety. Recording both sides before building the app raises the chance it will fit real clinic life instead of sitting unused.
plos-pone-0349344:
Guihong Tang, Safiah Omar, and Raida Abu Bakar translated a widely used work performance questionnaire into Chinese and checked whether it still measures properly. The survey rates three sides of job performance: doing core tasks well, helping the wider organisation, and behaviours that hold work back. Eight hundred and thirty-three Chinese workers completed the translated version for the validation.

Statistical checks confirmed the three-part structure, with strong, consistent item scores and a good overall fit. The questionnaire behaved the same for men and women, which makes group comparisons fair. Scores also lined up sensibly with a separate measure of human flourishing built around engagement, meaning, and accomplishment. The authors conclude that employers and researchers in China can now use this tool with confidence to study how people perform at work.
plos-pone-0349444:
After a dementia diagnosis, support usually trains staff and families, not the person diagnosed. Kate Gridley and colleagues studied a course made with and for people living with dementia, taught partly by peer tutors who have the condition themselves, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Working backward from outcomes, the team built a theory of how the course helps. Shared experience, equality in the room, and hopeful expectations set the stage. Then swapping stories and resources, learning led by peers, and taking on real roles did the work. Participants reported enjoyment, feeling valued, rebuilt social confidence, and a more positive view of life with dementia.
plos-pone-0349944:
Farhad Javanpour Heravi and co-authors model a heat sensor made of layered crystals in 2026. The layers are tungsten and silicon, stacked in a thin repeating pattern. Such stacks block sound waves in set bands. Those bands shift as heat changes, which is the sensing idea.

Five layouts were compared in simulation. Some used plain repeats, and others used near repeating patterns. One patterned layout opened the widest blocked band at the test heat. The plain layout, though, gave the steadiest and most even response to heat. Designers must weigh exotic layouts against plain ones that behave in a predictable way.
plos-pone-0350044:
Reddy and Gopinath, in a 2026 paper, present AgriOptNet, a framework that classifies soil texture from data and recommends crops based on soil nutrition. Farming advice is often slow, coarse, or too computing-heavy for field use. Their system blends a light neural network with several optimization tricks meant to keep it both accurate and fast.

One part sorts soil using a compact network stitched from three efficient designs, sharpened with attention steps. A feature picker, itself a hybrid of two animal-inspired search methods, keeps only the most telling soil measures. A learning agent then recommends crops and inputs, adjusting its advice as soil health, past yields, and surroundings change, with a bonus for exploring new options. The authors report the combined system beats older approaches on their tests. The paper is a design and benchmark report; farm trials would be the next test.
plos-pone-0350144:
Naruki Kitano and co-authors ran a wrist accelerometer survey of adults in three Japanese metro areas in 2026, and reported honestly on who took part. Movement surveys that need a device worn for days often fail on recruitment, skewing national figures.

Six hundred fifty adults were picked at random from resident registers, visited in person, and offered a cash incentive on completion. Only about three in ten responded, and slightly fewer wore the device enough days to count. Those who joined differed from census profiles. The paper's value is its candour: even best practice recruitment leaves gaps that analysts must admit.
plos-pone-0350644:
Job Agba Opue, Uchechukwu Emena Okorie, and Victor Ede Itita built a forecasting model for cholera and measles surges in ninety seven high burden Nigerian districts from 2018 to 2023. Shape based summaries of combined risk profiles, covering climate, conflict, displacement, and health system strain, were added to standard predictors in a boosting model with a four week horizon.

Shape aware models beat standard models by a clear margin on both diseases. Knowing the shape of a districts risk, not just its levels, added real warning power. In camps and conflict zones where data are messy, such structural clues could buy aid teams a month to pre position vaccines and water supplies.
plos-pone-0350744:
Jiafu Yang and co-authors built a scan based model in 2026 to predict a tumor marker in oesophageal cancer before surgery. The marker, CK19, hints at how invasive the cancer is, but today it is read only from tissue after removal.

Enhanced scans from one hundred thirty-four patients were mined for shape, texture, and brightness features, then fed to several learning methods. A random forest performed best on accuracy and precision among the rivals, and an explanation method showed which features drove its calls. A reliable pre surgery estimate could shape how wide surgery goes and how patients are counselled.
plos-pone-0350844:
Sudha Rani Unnam and Kareemulla Shaik built a computer security tool for small connected devices that talk through a low-power routing method called RPL. Their 2026 PLOS One paper tackles attacks that hijack these routes, a real risk because tiny devices cannot run heavy protective software.

Their system first picks the most telling data features with a kingfisher-inspired search method, then sorts traffic with a memory network that reads sequences forward and backward. Tested on a standard attack dataset covering four attack kinds, it spotted intrusions with accuracy above ninety-nine percent. The authors note the tests used simulated data, and training takes extra computing time.
plos-pone-0351244:
Gamze Alak surveyed just over five hundred adults in Turkey about autistic people: what they know, what contact they have had, and how at ease they feel interacting. Most contact reported was indirect, through media or acquaintances rather than close ties. Knowledge and comfort both scored fairly high overall, with gaps by age, schooling, and other background traits.

Comfort ran lower in social settings than at work, and lower when a persons support needs were higher. Knowledge carried the link between contact and comfort: contact helped when it built real understanding, and high quality contact mattered most. Programmes should aim for informed, meaningful contact, the author argues, not mere exposure.
plos-pone-0351544:
Silvia Timkova and colleagues examined the mouths of fifty-one professional soccer players from two elite Slovak clubs, pairing dentist inspections with saliva tests for gum-disease bacteria and gene variants. Athletes are a dental paradox, superfit yet plagued by decay and gum problems in study after study. Questionnaires covered habits, check-ups, and the sports drinks that bathe players' teeth in sugar and acid.

Almost all players had health insurance, yet over a third had skipped the dentist for a year. Brushing was diligent, twice daily or more for most, but fewer than half cleaned between teeth, and over four in five drank sugary sports drinks. The picture is of routines defeated by schedule and habit, not ignorance. Clubs employ doctors for hamstrings; this audit argues a dentist belongs on the same staff list.
plos-pone-0351644:
Yan and colleagues, in a 2026 archaeology study, map how settlements gathered and moved around China's Songshan Mountains across six thousand years, from early farming villages to the Bronze Age. The region is a cradle of early Chinese civilization. Nearly two thousand sites from four cultural phases were analyzed with mapping and clustering tools.

Settlements stayed clustered in every period, bunching tightest in the last phase. The densest zones crept westward over time, ending in a two-center pattern around two modern cities. Even as site numbers grew fivefold, the best cluster count fell from nine to two, a sign of scattered villages knitting into larger political wholes. Early on, land and water set the pattern. By the last phase, political pull seems to have mattered more, holding people together even as the climate worsened. The authors offer their open method for other regions.
plos-pone-0351744:
Yanming Zhu and three colleagues apply space syntax analysis to the public spaces of a historic Chinese city, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Meizhou Ancient City in Guangdong faces familiar problems: single-purpose spaces, tangled road links, and layouts that confuse visitors and residents alike. The team measured how connected and readable the street and square network is, then paired the numbers with field research.

Their diagnosis led to a strategy of merging scattered assets, rebuilding functions, and fixing awkward junctions between spaces. After the proposed intervention, their models showed public spaces working together better and the district coping better with change. The authors present the method as a transferable template for historic cities under development pressure.
plos-pone-0351844:
Abeer Aloufi and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a silver-selenium particle mix. The mix was brewed with melon peel extract, a green way to make it. The team checked the blend's structure with several tools, and found mostly round particles. They tested it on cancer cells and on normal cells. They also tested it on clinical samples of a drug-resistant germ, a form of staph that shrugs off a key antibiotic.

The particles harmed two cancer cell lines at far lower doses than normal lung cells. That hints at selective toxicity. Against the resistant germs, the mix killed well and tore cell membranes. It also slowed biofilm growth, though results varied by strain. Mixing it with the old drug helped only at times. The authors present the blend as a promising dual-purpose candidate that needs more work.
plos-pone-0351944:
Syed Rehman Jamil and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study using machine learning to predict how industrial cooling towers perform. Cooling towers dump waste heat for factories, and their efficiency and water use depend on inlet water temperature, air temperature, and humidity. The team trained four algorithms on operating data to forecast outlet water temperature, water losses, effectiveness, and thermodynamic efficiency.

A support vector machine proved most accurate of the four. The analysis showed that humid air sharply cuts evaporation losses and the makeup water a tower needs, while warmer air improved the tower's second-law efficiency. The authors present predictive modeling as a practical way to run towers with less water and better performance.
plos-pone-0352144:
Wentao Wu used forty years of simulated weather and farming to find cropping plans for northern China that yield well without heavy emissions. Three rotations were compared, from single spring maize to a wheat and maize double crop and a triple crop, each under four nitrogen fertilizer levels. A crop model replayed the years day by day, tracking harvests, soil carbon, and nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

More fertilizer generally raised yields and soil carbon, but it also pushed emissions up year after year. The best balance came from the wheat and summer maize double crop paired with a moderate fertilizer rate, which topped the study's climate resilience index. For the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the point is that the winning recipe is a matched pair, the rotation and the dose chosen together, not either one alone.
plos-pone-0352244:
Yong He and co-authors improve a detection model in 2026. The model finds small objects in drone photos. Busy backgrounds make those targets hard to spot. The upgrade adds a finer head for tiny targets. It also adds a fusion module based on frequency views. That module mixes wave pooling with attention steps.

A lighter backbone was built from faster blocks. Those blocks can be reshaped for fast use. Tests used a public drone dataset with many scenes. The new model raised the main accuracy score clearly. It also cut the parameter count by a quarter. Computing cost rose by about a third. The authors call the trade good for patrol and rescue work.
plos-pone-0352344:
Laura Frederiksen and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study of extra infections in patients admitted to an Australian hospital in 2022 with COVID-19 classed as moderate to severe. Knowing how often bacteria, fungi, or other viruses join the initial infection matters for antibiotic decisions. The team reviewed one hundred ninety admissions, comparing patients with and without documented coinfection.

Only about one in eight patients had a coinfection, most often bacterial, yet three-quarters received antibiotics, typically for six days. Patients with coinfection stayed in hospital longer, though death rates did not differ. Intensive care patients and those with severe disease were more likely to have coinfection. The authors call the antibiotic use disproportionate and urge better testing so treatment matches actual infection.
plos-pone-0352444:
Shanza Zaib and seven colleagues ask how forest soil fungi weather a drought-and-downpour cycle. Their 2026 study sits in managed beech forests of central Slovakia. An eighteen-day dry spell ended with heavy rain. Soil was sampled just before the rain and seven days after. Both the litter layer and the mineral soil below were tested. DNA barcoding identified the fungi, and an enzyme assay gauged decomposition potential.

Depth, not rain, ran the show. Litter and mineral soil held clearly different fungal communities. Root-linked fungi and soil decomposers ruled the mineral layer. Pathogens and litter specialists crowded the surface. The rewetting changed nothing detectable within a week. Community mix, diversity, and enzyme activity all held steady. Forest fungi may simply shrug off single short drought cycles. Longer or repeated extremes remain the open question this baseline helps frame.
plos-pone-0352644:
Jason Maikos and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One trial of prosthetic ankle-foot devices. The users had below-knee limb loss. Ninety-one people took part, a mix of veterans, service members, and civilians. Each person tried three device types in random order. One was a springy energy-returning foot. One was an articulating foot. One was a powered foot. Each got a week of adjustment time. Thirteen people without limb loss gave reference values.

Lab gait measures were by far the most sensitive to device type. Nineteen measures differed, mostly at the ankle. Timed walking and mobility tests showed no clear device effect. Survey scores split in a telling way. Measured gait looked most natural on the powered foot. Yet users said they preferred the simpler non-powered devices. The authors say prescriptions should weigh both kinds of proof for each person.
plos-pone-0352744:
Fei Hao and co-authors build a drone-based system for naming desert grassland plants from the air when only a handful of labeled examples exist. Desert rangelands need watching for ecological security, and hyperspectral cameras see species-level detail, but training data are scarce. Their method learns how to learn. One branch reads fine local texture. A second, sequence-based branch reads wide spatial patterns. A meta-learning routine then teaches the pair to adapt from few examples.

Across test scenes the system classified species with accuracy above ninety percent on headline measures and stayed steady as sample sizes shrank. Hao and colleagues present it as a practical route for agencies that must map fragile rangelands without funding huge labeling campaigns first.
plos-pone-0352944:
This entry is a formal retraction notice issued by the PLOS One editors in 2026, withdrawing an earlier article that claimed a receptor called GPR91 helps drive heart enlargement under pressure overload. Readers should not rely on the original article's conclusions. The editors acted after concerns were raised about the paper's overlap with a previously published article by a partly shared author group, which the paper never cited.

Both articles studied the same signaling pathway in the same animal model and reported similar methods, results, and conclusions. The notice also lists figure problems, including unexplained symbols and unlabeled panels, a missing ethics approval number, and anesthesia practices that may not have met accepted standards. The first author maintained the two papers differed in scope, but the editors retracted the article.
plos-pone-0353244:
Zhou and colleagues, in a 2026 engineering study, test a new connector that ties steel facade panels to a building's frame. Prefabricated steel walls need joints that are strong, cheap, and easy to fit on site. Their design grouts a stud inside a small steel tube, borrowing from sleeve grouting used elsewhere in construction. Eighteen test pieces were pulled until they failed, and computer models replayed the tests.

Strain grew from the stud's ends outward, and the models matched the real failures closely. The connector held up well even with weak grout and a shallow stud embedment, which cuts cost and eases site work. A formula the team derived for the load at which the connector yields predicted test results with small error. The authors offer the detail and its design math as a ready option for prefabricated steel facades, filling a gap in standards.
plos-pone-0353344:
Li and colleagues compared nurse-led sedation care for patients on breathing machines in a 2026 study. Keeping patients calm but not too deeply asleep helps them leave the ventilator sooner. Records from one intensive care unit over two years split patients into usual doctor-led care and a nurse-led plan with daily targets and frequent checks.

Patients under nurse-led care spent less time on the ventilator and fewer days in intensive care. Signs of too-deep or too-light sedation also fell. Confusion rates were lower but not clearly so, and death rates did not differ. Structured nurse control of sedation looks like a safe way to free patients from machines sooner.
plos-pone-0353744:
Fang Chen and seven colleagues characterise a long non-coding RNA that runs high in lung adenocarcinoma, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These RNAs do not build proteins but steer other genes. Found through public cancer datasets and confirmed in tumour cell lines, the RNA — known by the code RP3-340N1.2 — was dialled down in laboratory experiments to see what the cancer cells would do.

Silencing it slowed the cells' growth, movement, invasion, and colony formation, and shrank tumours grown in mice. The RNA appears to work by soaking up a small regulatory RNA, freeing a signalling protein that feeds a growth pathway. Restoring that protein's activity reversed the silencing effect. The chain is a candidate target for future lung cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0353844:
Yolacan, in a 2026 mathematics paper, introduces a new kind of mapping for cleaning up blurred signals and images. The work sits in fixed point theory, the study of processes that settle by repeating a step. The new mapping blends a known family with a directed graph, and the paper proves that a two-step repeating method built on it converges.

Proof alone is not the whole story: the method was tried on standard blurred images spoiled by motion blur and random noise. It restored them with quality scores that beat three classical methods and matched a leading edge-preserving approach. On one-dimensional signals it did even better, with high scores on both sharpness and structural likeness to the original. Yolacan presents the framework as a mathematically grounded addition to the deblurring toolbox, with its strength proven rather than merely observed.
plos-pone-0353944:
Farzaneh Ramezani, Farzaneh Saki, and Mohammad Reza Zoghi Paydar present a protocol, published in 2026, for a trial of brain-and-body training. The training aims to protect female volleyball players' knees. Players whose knees collapse inward on landing face high risk of tearing the anterior cruciate ligament. A spike or quick cut must often be decided in a split second, under divided attention.

The planned eight-week trial will randomize players aged eighteen to twenty-three with confirmed inward knee collapse. One group gets standard neuromuscular training. The other gets the same training fused with cognitive challenges that mimic game pressure. Landing mechanics will be filmed under calm and distracted conditions. Brain activity, muscle firing, balance, and strength will be tracked too. The design targets the game-real moment when injuries actually happen.
plos-pone-0354144:
Md Riyadh Arefin and six colleagues flood tea plants to find which varieties survive waterlogged soil, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Bangladesh. Tea earnings matter greatly to the country, and erratic rains increasingly drown the bushes. Eight candidate genotypes plus two standard clones endured two weeks under water, then two weeks of recovery, while twenty-three growth and chemistry traits were measured.

Flooding cut photosynthesis, leaf numbers, and root weight, while protective chemicals rose in leaves and roots. Comparing stress-tolerance scores separated the hardy lines from the fragile ones. The authors argue that breeding from the tolerant genotypes is the practical route to tea harvests that survive a wetter climate.
plos-pone-0354244:
Aneesa Rasheed Anwar and three co-authors turn fruit peel waste into a water-holding gel for dry farms, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The work responds to the United Arab Emirates' harsh conditions: scarce water, poor soil, and heavy reliance on chemical fertiliser. They extracted pectin from orange peel and starch from banana peel, then linked them into soft gels using calcium and a common synthetic polymer.

Laboratory checks confirmed the raw materials were pure and stable, and microscope images showed a well-connected, porous structure suited to soaking up water. Such gels could store rain or irrigation water in soil and release it slowly, cutting waste in arid farming.
plos-pone-0354344:
Seline Verbaan led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a randomized trial preparing older patients for leg artery surgery. People over sixty-five with severely blocked leg arteries face long hospital stays and poor recovery. The planned Dutch trial will enroll three hundred patients across centers for a combined program of exercise, nutrition, and support before their operation, or usual care.

Outcomes span hospital stay, complications, patient reports, and costs. As a protocol it reports a plan, not findings. Verbaan's team designed it to settle whether prehabilitation belongs in routine vascular care.
plos-pone-0354744:
Shalinder Sabherwal and colleagues present in 2026 a full picture of eye care need and service capacity in one catchment area. They paired a population survey of avoidable blindness in older adults with a new module that checks what local providers actually offer. People aged fifty and above were examined in large numbers.

Blindness was more common in women, and unoperated cataract caused most blindness and severe loss. Glasses coverage was low, especially for women, and records on surgery and diabetes eye care were patchy across providers. Linking need to capacity this way, the authors argue, gives planners a firmer base than either source alone.
plos-pone-0355044:
Carolina Messer-Soubelet, Bernardo Riffo, and Omar Barriga build a questionnaire to measure how well school professionals read minds, their own and others', when teaching children with autism. This mind-reading capacity shapes classroom inclusion, yet it is usually studied in clinics, not staff rooms. Nearly three hundred professionals in Chilean schools with inclusion policies completed the new self-report tool, whose structure the team probed with factor analysis.

The answers settled into a multi-part scale grouped under two broad domains: spotting others' mental states and spotting one's own. Early reliability checks supported the tool. Messer-Soubelet and colleagues offer it as a first step toward training that treats perspective skills as something schools can measure and grow, rather than assume.
plos-pone-0355244:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing a global review that had pooled trials of integrated palliative care against standard care for cancer patients. Readers should not rely on that review's pooled findings. The main problem was a basic statistical error in how effects were calculated and combined.

Effects figured as simple mean differences were reported as standardised differences, though studies used different scales, so one unit did not mean the same thing across studies. Data extraction for several included studies was also in doubt, and some study labels could not be traced at first. An independent statistical adviser judged the error likely changed the findings greatly.
plos-pone-0355544:
Emre Karaduman and co-authors studied how fear of COVID-19 related to coping among one thousand female university students after the emergency phase. Fear was the pandemic's central emotion, yet its link with coping in this group was unclear. Their 2026 survey measured fear levels and outbreak coping strategies with standard scales.

Greater fear came with more active coping, not less. Two experiences changed that relationship's strength. Being physically active moderated the link, and so did having personally tested positive or negative for the virus. Karaduman and colleagues suggest habits like regular exercise, and firsthand infection experience, keep shaping fear and coping long after the crisis headlines fade.
plos-pone-0355744:
Hao Liu and seven colleagues examine a hard call in HIV care in this 2026 study from seven Chinese medical centers. Some patients on treatment keep a small but persistent amount of virus in their blood, too low to count as failure yet too high to ignore. Doctors disagree on whether switching their drug regimen helps, so the team looked back at real-world records for just over one hundred sixty such patients.

About two thirds of patients who switched regimens had fully suppressed virus a year later, nearly the same share as those who stayed on their original drugs. Virus levels drifted down and immune cell counts rose modestly in both groups, with no clear advantage for switching. The authors say the results argue against switching automatically, though they note the study's modest size and retrospective design.
plos-pone-0355844:
Hamis Daniel Wambura, Gration Mutashoberwa Rwegasira, and Martin John Martin survey what drives infestation by the African sugarcane stalk borer in Tanzania. The moth larva tunnels cane stalks and can cut yields steeply while draining sugar content. Teams sampled hundreds of field blocks across low, middle, and high elevations in both seasons, counting larvae and damage in random stalk bundles from each block.

the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-daisy-cha: Charlotte Yonge's The Trial continues the beloved story of the Daisy Chain. The sorely tried May family faces new sorrows and duties. Steadfast faith carries them through every loss. A cherished sequel for Victorian readers.
